title: Broadway’s ‘Galileo’ Adds Cast: Javier Muñoz, Bradley Dean Join Raúl Esparza; ‘Stranger Things’ Actor Michael Park To Alternate Lead
full_text: Skip to main content By Greg Evans Greg Evans NY & Broadway Editor @GregEvans5 More Stories By Greg Krysta Rodriguez Joins ‘A Few Good Men’ Broadway Revival Starring Bradley Whitford And Tom Blyth; Complete Cast & Creative Team Announced ‘Moulin Rouge!’ With Aaron Tveit Bids Adieu With Best Gross In Years – Broadway Box Office Miley Cyrus Announces New ‘Bass Persuades’ Album, Two Hollywood Bowl Shows; Drops Last Name View All September 2, 2026 6:28am Production Broadway ‘s upcoming Galileo musical starring Raúl Esparza also will feature Bradley Dean ( Chess ), Jordon Lee Garcia (Broadway debut) and Javier Muñoz ( Hamilton, In the Heights ), producers announced today. Also joining the cast is Michael Park ( Stranger Things, As the World Turns ), who will alternate with Esparza in the title role at certain performances. The new musical, inspired by the life of groundbreaking astronomer and scientist Galileo Galilei, begins performances at the Shubert Theatre on Tuesday, November 10, with an opening night set for Sunday evening, December 6. Related Stories News Krysta Rodriguez Joins 'A Few Good Men' Broadway Revival Starring Bradley Whitford And Tom Blyth; Complete Cast & Creative Team Announced News 'Moulin Rouge!' With Aaron Tveit Bids Adieu With Best Gross In Years - Broadway Box Office The castings were announced by producers Amanda Lipitz, Henry Tisch and Jordan Roth. In addition to Esparza, previously announced cast members include Jeremy Kushnier and Tony Joy Woods. The musical features a book by Danny Strong and an original score by Zoe Sarnak and Michael Weiner, and will be directed by Michael Mayer and choreographed by David Neumann. Watch on Deadline Additional information, including complete casting, will be announced shortly. The synopsis: “When luminary Galileo (Esparza) peers into the heavens, what he sees challenges humanity’s understanding of the world. Unwilling to deny the truth, Galileo finds himself in a fight with the most powerful institution on Earth. As his trusted confidant Barberini (Kushnier) ascends to power, friendship leads to betrayal, and the dreams Galileo has envisioned for himself and for his brilliant daughter Virginia (Woods) begin to slip away. Belief, ambition, and love pull the trio out of orbit, each confronting what they’re willing to sacrifice for what matters most.” Baz Bamigboye Looks Back On Tabloid Life With ‘Ink’s Danny Boyle & James Graham Alexander Opens Film Arm With Kevin Chan & Hamish Moseley On Board Tom Cruise Backs WBD Deal & CEO’s Vow Of 30 Pics A Year: “It’s Awesome” Taneo Sebastian Cast In Don Josephus Raphael Eblahan’s ‘Hum’ Read More About: Comments

title: Chilean Alfredo Castro-Led Dark Comedy ‘After Elena’ World Premieres at Toronto Film Fest, Bows Trailer (EXCLUSIVE)
full_text: Sep 2, 2026 6:24am PT Chilean Alfredo Castro-Led Dark Comedy ‘After Elena’ World Premieres at Toronto Film Fest, Bows Trailer (EXCLUSIVE) By Anna Marie de la Fuente Plus Icon Anna Marie de la Fuente @adelafuente1 Latest Martin Scorsese Mentee Celina Murga Preps Next Pic, ‘The Rehearsals’ 7 hours ago Chile’s Sanfic-Morbido Lab Launches WomanInFan Southern Cone Alliance With Sitges Film Fest and Fantastic WIP (EXCLUSIVE) 1 day ago Mexico’s Martfilms Boards ‘Looking for Sam,’ Mariana Rondón’s Follow-Up to ‘Bad Hair’ (EXCLUSIVE) 1 day ago See All 'After Elena' Courtesy of Meikincine Chile’s everyman actor Alfredo Castro (“The Count”) plays against type in “After Elena” (“Después de Elena”) by Shawn Garry, which world premieres at the Toronto Film Festival ( TIFF ) on Sept.11. Bowing a trailer and poster exclusively in Variety, “After Elena” “shows Castro in a completely different register from what we’ve seen him in before and the cast also includes Nicolás Zárate (“Red Hangar”), who has won multiple awards this year,” said Gabriela Sandoval who produced the dark family comedy out of her label Cine Matriz. Related Stories Owner of L.A. Rams and Denver Nuggets Buys Los Angeles Angels Baseball Team Miley Cyrus Announces New Album 'Bass Persuades,' Sets Two Shows for Hollywood Bowl The rest of the cast include Carola Varleta and Guilherme Sepúlveda while Catalina Saavedra – who took home an acting prize at Sundance for her gripping debut performance in 2009 Chilean drama, “The Maid”– plays a small but pivotal role. Popular on Variety Castro plays 70-year-old Roberto whose beloved wife Elena has died. He wants nothing more than to retreat into his lifelong home. But when an economic and emotional crisis drives his three adult children back under his roof, old wounds, buried secrets and simmering tensions resurface. As they navigate their grief, the family must find a way to reconnect or risk tearing itself apart. The trailer opens with Castro’s character, the recently widowed Roberto, waking up to a phone call in the middle of the night to news that one of his sons has tried to kill himself. Chaos ensues as all three adult kids and their offspring move in. The multi-country co-production includes Colombia’s Doc: Co, Garry’s own label Creative Content, Italy’s Zoe Films, Fundacion Rio and By Lace Films. Buenos Aires-based boutique sales agency Meikincine Entertainment boarded the film at the development stage. In an earlier interview, Sandoval explained what drew them to this project: “We were attracted by the possibility of addressing themes such as old age, death, grief and family trauma, but from a different perspective: not as a conventional drama, but through dark humor and absurdity as a narrative vehicle.” Castro has frequently collaborated with Pablo Larrain (“Jackie,” “The Club”) where he played dramatic roles in such gems as “Tony Manero,” “No,” “The Club” and most recently, “The Count.” Larrain’s feature-length spin-off from his Netflix mini-series “My Sad Dead,” competes at the San Sebastian Film Festival where it world premieres. “After Elena” is the sophomore feature of Chilean director-producer Shawn Garry that follows his debut, “Desierto Sur.” He co-wrote the dramedy with writer-director Bernardo Quesney (“History y Geography”) and Carla Stagno (“Allende, The Thousand Days”). title: Rupert Murdoch Was “Very Happy” With the Casting of Danny Boyle’s ‘Ink’
full_text: × Skip to main content By Scott Roxborough Plus Icon Scott Roxborough Europe Bureau Chief sroxborough Follow Sign Up View All September 2, 2026 6:08am 'Ink' Courtesy of Netflix Rupert Murdoch and the world of British tabloid journalism were in the spotlight in Venice on Tuesday as Danny Boyle presented his new film Ink , which opens the 83rd Biennale Wednesday night. The film, adapted from James Graham’s stage play, depicts Murdoch’s entry into the British newspaper scene, when he acquired the then-failing tabloid The Sun in 1969. Hiring Larry Lamb as editor, the two combined far-right political reporting and populist rabble to turn the paper into a dark force in British media. Murdoch would take the lessons learned at The Sun and apply them to build his U.S. media empire with The New York Post and Fox News. Related Stories Movies George Clooney Tells Venice Studios Are Making Movies That "Need a Launchpad of a Film Festival Less and Less" Movies Slavoj Zizek on Why We Seek Utopias in the Movies (Exclusive Trailer) Guy Pearce plays Murdoch. Jack O’Connell ( Sinners ) plays Lamb. Claire Foy ( The Crown , Women Talking ) co-stars as Jules Davies, an amalgam of female executives who worked under Lamb at The Sun and a character new to the film adaptation. Boyle said during a press conference that he was careful, as with the stage version not to “monsterize” Rupert Murdoch “because he represented at the time [a] breath of fresh air in what was a very rigid British society. It begins with something that’s fun and different, challenging a rigid order… It was important to us that the audience feels complicit.” Foy said she found plunging into the world of ‘60s tabloid journalism “really intoxicating,” admitting to feeling “quite jealous” of Fleet Street reporters. “They had power at their fingertips. They knew what they wrote would be what people read and what people believed.” Pearce revealed that Murdoch himself was pleased with the film’s casting. “I had some messaging with Elizabeth [Murdoch], his daughter, and she said ‘Dad’s very happy that you are playing him.’ But he hadn’t seen the film at that point.” Graham said Murdoch had, however, caught the original play. “He came to see the play twice,” he recalled, though he didn’t give his opinion of the story. “He’s very good at not giving anything away which I think is one of his secrets.” Though the film is set in the 1960s, Boyle said he wasn’t as interested in making a period piece, arguing that Ink was “about the modern world” showing many of the trends in the media that shape the current world. As divisive as Rupert Murdoch and The Sun were, and are, Boyle argued, the father of modern tabloid journalism was, at his heart, “a print man” who he thinks must be “driven to despair” at the disappearance of the print industry, “the tactile world that we used to depend on to read the stories about us.” Boyle ended the press conference with an extolment of the value of journalism that “speaks truth to power,” calling it “one of great uprights of any civilization.” He also acknowledged the great threats facing journalists, print or otherwise, in the age of AI. “The danger with the tech giants, obviously [is that] they’ll be able to have an AI journalist who’s much more efficient, lot cheaper, etc. etc.,” the director said. “But will that AI journalist speak truth to that power that’s created it? That’s going to be very very tough.” Ink is screening in competition in Venice. The film will release in select theaters in the U.S. on Dec. 11 before going out on Netflix on Jan. 8 in the U.S. and Latin America. Studiocanal is releasing the film theatrically across multiple territories, including the U.K., France, Germany, Poland, Australia and New Zealand, starting with the U.K. release on Jan. 8. Studiocanal is also handling worldwide sales, and is co-representing domestic with WME Independent. THR

title: Travis Kelce Details “Insane” Wedding to Taylor Swift: “Biggest Night of Our Lives”
full_text: × Skip to main content By Lily Ford Plus Icon Lily Ford @lilyfordtweets Follow Sign Up View All September 2, 2026 6:01am Swift and Kelce photographed in 2025. Courtesy of Getty Travis Kelce is officially, as he puts it, “a married man.” The Kansas City Chiefs tight end was beaming to his brother, Jason, in a new episode of their New Heights podcast on Wednesday, where Kelce spoke in depth for the first time about that all-star, ludicrously lavish wedding ceremony to pop queen Taylor Swift on July 3. “It’s been so much fun, it was insane,” said Kelce about the event at Madison Square Garden, with a guest list that boasted Jack Antonoff, Bradley Cooper, Lena Dunham, Selena Gomez, Ed Sheeran, Dakota Johnson, Jason Sudeikis, Benson Boone, Hugh Grant, Kelsea Ballerini, Camila Cabello, Karlie Kloss and Josh Kushner, Ethan Hawke, Zoë Kravitz, Mariska Hargitay and Peter Hermann and the Haim sisters, among hundreds of other A-listers. Related Stories Music Harry Styles Jokes About Taylor Swift's Wedding During Madison Square Garden Concert Music Taylor Swift Remembers Dolly Parton's "True Grace and Grit": "Her Legacy Will Be Everlasting" Kelce said it was a night that he and his Grammy-winning wife, who began dating in 2023, will never forget. “Me and Taylor are so thankful for everybody that showed up. From the vows to seeing everyone to how much fun we had throughout the entire evening, and hearing that being relayed through everyone’s stories of that night… It was just so magical, man. I wish it could have lasted longer than it did.” He also gave a shout-out to Hollywood actor Adam Sandler, who officiated the ceremony. “He has been just the fucking best person on this planet,” said Kelce. “For him to be up for getting ordained in the state of New York and marrying me and Taylor, and the way he did it, in the very Sandman style, and giving us more than what we could’ve imagined at that moment, knowing that it was the biggest night of our lives, it was absolutely insane man.” The football star joked that at the end of the ceremony, “once the drinks stopped being served, everyone [started] to mosey out.” He continued: “But thank you to everyone at MSG… We wanted it to do it somewhere where we could have a very intimate and genuine setting without a lot of distractions and we needed to have a private feel, and MSG went above and beyond to give us that and I can’t thank everybody enough, that showed up but helped put that show on.” Eyebrows were certainly raised when rumors of the MSG wedding gained traction. It proved to be a savvy move from Swift and Kelce as intense security and privacy measures were undertaken. On Thursday, ahead of the rehearsal dinner, The Hollywood Reporter spotted a white tent being raised up to the door of the VIP entrance to the arena. In front of the Garden’s main entrance, THR heard that another, red curtain had gone up. Police officers were stationed in packs around the venue, particularly on 7th and 8th Avenues. Snipers were stationed atop MSG, with surveillance helicopters heard overhead. Numerous streets around the arena were also closed to vehicles and, in some cases, pedestrian traffic. The guests themselves remained enshrouded in secrecy as black cars were seen driving into a large white tent, with the entrance set off by black curtains, shielding attendees from nearby prying eyes. We’re still waiting on those hotly-anticipated photos from the wedding — it remains to be seen if the couple will ever release footage or images from inside the event — but their team did confirm on July 2 that the superstar singer-songwriter and her then-fiancé had made $26 million in charitable donation s to more than a dozen organizations across the country. THR revealed that Swift wore a custom haute couture gown by Jonathan Anderson of Christian Dior. Kelce also wore a haute couture look by Anderson for Dior. The event marked the first time Anderson has designed a couture wedding dress for a celebrity of Swift’s stature, and both the bride and groom wore Christian Louboutin shoes. Swift wore Cartier jewellery. THR

title: Rupert Murdoch ‘Is Very Happy’ Guy Pearce Is Playing Him in ‘Ink’; Actor Says Mogul’s Daughter Shared Praise
full_text: Sep 2, 2026 6:00am PT Rupert Murdoch ‘Is Very Happy’ Guy Pearce Is Playing Him in ‘Ink’; Actor Says Mogul’s Daughter Shared Praise By Ellise Shafer , Elsa Keslassy Michael Buckner Rupert Murdoch is apparently “very happy” that he’s being played by Guy Pearce in Danny Boyle’s “Ink.” During the movie’s press conference at the Venice Film Festival on Wednesday, Pearce was asked along with Boyle and screenwriter James Graham if they had spoken to Murdoch about the film. Though Pearce said he hadn’t made contact with the mogul himself, he revealed that he reached out to Murdoch’s daughter, Elisabeth Murdoch. Related Stories Martin Scorsese Mentee Celina Murga Preps Next Pic, ‘The Rehearsals’ Julianne Moore to Receive Zurich's Golden Icon Award as Jesse Eisenberg's 'The Debut' Screens “She did say to me, ‘Dad’s very happy that you’re playing him,'” Pearce said. “But he hadn’t seen the film at that point, so we’ll see.” Popular on Variety “Ink,” which opens the festival on Wednesday night and is competing for the Golden Lion, takes place in 1969 as Murdoch acquires the struggling Sun and installs Larry Lamb (Jack O’Connell) as editor with the mission of overtaking its dominant rival, the Daily Mirror. Graham, who also wrote the Tony-winning play on which the movie is based, said that Murdoch is familiar with the story as he came to see the play twice, both on the West End and Broadway. “I remember he was very good at sort of not really giving anything away,” Graham said of Murdoch’s reaction. However, he remembers him enjoying a particular sequence that showed the printing press and “the dirt and the steam and the filth that used to go into making a paper on a daily basis.” Graham added, “I think he’ll be very flattered by the casting.” “Ink” marks Boyle’s first appearance at the Venice Film Festival. The Oscar-winning director arrives on the Lido following his return to the zombie franchise he helped create with “28 Years Later.” His credits also include “Trainspotting,” “127 Hours,” “Steve Jobs” and “Slumdog Millionaire,” which won eight Oscars, including best picture and best director. Elsewhere during the press conference, Boyle pointed out that “Ink” “doesn’t monsterize Rupert Murdoch, which of course a lot of people do now.” He added, “I think it’s because he represented at the time a breath of fresh air in what was a very rigid British society … he offered a kind of freedom with a different voice, really.” But Murdoch and Lamb also both have a “darkness” that Boyle said his film explores more than in the play. “In the stage play, the darkness is reported off stage, and yet I knew in cinema you would see it,” Boyle said. “And then you have to find an actor that can take you there.” He noted that O’Connell “has that ability to take you into dark places with him, like Pacino in ‘Godfather 2,'” causing a surprised expression to come across O’Connell’s face. “He’s going to hate me saying that,” Boyle added with a smirk. Netflix acquired U.S. and Latin American rights to “Ink” shortly after it was announced as Venice’s opening film. Studiocanal, which produced the movie with Media Res and House Productions, is releasing it theatrically across several territories including the U.K., France, Germany and Italy. Boyle produced “Ink” with Tessa Ross, Michael Ellenberg and Tracey Seaward. title: Elon Musk Unmasked in Alex Gibney Documentary: “Insane a Person This Chaotic Has So Much Power”
full_text: Skip to main content Illustration by Robert Carter Late one August afternoon in a Manhattan editing suite, with thunder and lightning raging outside, a storm was also brewing inside. Or at least on the giant screen at the front of the room. “How’s power feeling, Mr. Musk?” a bystander calls out to Elon Musk onscreen as the beaming tech mogul strides through a post-inauguration Washington building. In the next scene, Musk sits at a roundtable with his army of early 20s DOGE staffers, looking on proudly alongside Fox News’ Jesse Watters. The young men talk with easy, deluded confidence about how they will fix government as Watters jokingly refers to the notoriously anatomical nickname of one of the men. Related Stories Movies Forget the Red Carpet -- Venice's Real Stars Are in the Documentaries This Year Movies Alex Gibney's Elon Musk Doc Will Play TIFF, Setting the Stage for an Epic Culture Wars Battle Illustration by Robert Carter At the back of the editing room, Alex Gibney , the longtime documentarian and the closest the current film world has to a Bob Woodward, watches intently. “Let’s do that ‘power’ quote hotter,” Gibney says to a team of five that includes his frequent producer Erin Edeiken and sound mixer Tony Volante. “Hotter? Yes,” Volante says, adjusting levels on the screen in front of him. Gibney has been working since late 2022 trying to get a temperature read on Musk only to see the mercury continue to climb. He had finished — or thought he had finished — a two-hour HBO documentary on Musk in late 2024, having plumbed the controversial entrepreneur’s childhood, his early PayPal-ish forays into Silicon Valley, his supercharging of SpaceX, his takeover of Tesla, his launching of the satellites of Starlink, his hirings and firings at Neuralink, his bull run into Twitter, his various mad dashes through wives and baby mamas, and many other events that would make most humans seek out a long, uninterrupted Xanax vacation. Then Musk donated ungodly sums and made appearances to help deliver the presidency to Donald Trump, who returned the favor by giving Musk the Chewbacca seat on the Millennium Falcon. Suddenly the story seemed to hold another chapter. HBO executives called Gibney telling him they wanted and would finance more. He kept shooting. And shot some more. For nearly two additional years, all the way to a six-hour cut of the movie that went deep on Musk’s 2025 DOGE era and his SpaceX IPO plate-spin this summer. (The film has since been cut down.) Over the course of a decorated career, Gibney, 72, had taken on Scientology and Enron, the U.S. military and Vladimir Putin, the Catholic Church and Wall Street. All of that prepared him, though nothing could really prepare him, for this magnum Musk creation — cinema’s premier curtain-puller on power revealing the man who has amassed so much of it. When it comes out this fall, Musk will look to change the game in several crucial ways, lining up a target that Hollywood never shoots at, seeking to become a hit documentary in an era allergic to them and trying to open the eyes of American voters to a key Republican electoral arms dealer who Gibney says is mounting an unfair fight. At stake with Musk, its creator wants to tell us, is nothing less than the future of democracy. And to spread that message, he has enlisted some of the biggest media companies around — including, improbably enough, the one soon to be owned by Trump ally David Ellison. Today, Gibney is making small tweaks to finish the film in time for screenings at the Venice and Toronto film festivals in September (three hours, 45 minutes), a wide theatrical release in October (ditto) and an HBO debut in 2027 (four hours). There are sounds to adjust and effects to complete and even video game reenactments to perfect. What better way to take on a maximalist than maximally? The sound on the DOGE scene in front of him calibrated, Gibney gives a small look of approval. “Great,” he says. “Now let’s go to Watters and Big Balls.” *** Elon Musk is not an obvious candidate for a documentary. A documentary aims to tell us something new, and Elon Musk epitomizes the familiar. We take stock of his trolls on X, we see him artwash his image on Saturday Night Live , we get a load of his engineering and entrepreneurial genius from biographer Walter Isaacson, we learn about his stock market genius on CNBC, we hear him talk about the goal of further populating the planet, we hear one example after another of his personal efforts in pursuit of that goal, we eye with skepticism his proclaiming the age of Mars colonization and extraterrestrial data centers, we watch him (and then try to unwatch him) gleefully talk of slashing-and-burning aid workers from inside White House meeting rooms. So much Musk have we ambiently ingested these past few years that perhaps the best cultural gift might be a break from all that, an Elon-free zone populated with anyone besides the 55-year-old provocateur. Yet Gibney aggressively wants to challenge that instinct, and he may have a point. None of what we have seen and thought about Musk can fully ready us for what the filmmaker has done here — an adventurous but methodical movie grounded in the thesis that, as he sees it, a dangerous huckster is stealthily aggregating power to exploit us, primarily by centralizing and controlling massive amounts of data. Gibney’s basic take on Musk is that he’s a confidence man whose power comes only from the stock market and disappears the minute we see through the facade of sales pitches — but can do a whole lot of damage until that happens. The film world-premieres Sept. 8 at Venice. But its cultural reach will likely extend far beyond that. Musk stands poised to touch off a fresh wave of anger and fear among the millions already inclined to worry about him, into and well after the midterms, while fueling a whole lot of trollishness (and worse?) from the many who worship at the temple of Elon Musk, including Elon Musk. Gibney has crafted a movie that, while not new in its specifics, is often damning in its totality, standing apart from anything the media entertainment complex has recently turned out — a portrait of power with the cinematic scope of All the King’s Men and the potential social impact of The Pentagon Papers . (“It’s rare these days to see a complete story instead of the fragments we’re used to,” says Anonymous Content’s Nick Shumaker, a producer on the film.) Some will surely find Musk overly negative and conspiratorial. Yet nearly every time the film seems like it might tip into paranoid fantasy, Gibney unearths a new fact or asks a new commonsense question to steady us back. Gibney spends the first half of the film coming at Musk for various alleged sins, including stealing credit from original Tesla founder Martin Eberhard; bullying a woman who birthed his child to sign an NDA; pumping his stocks with shaky talk of Mars exploration and full self-driving cars (the latter of which Gibney also alleges are responsible for more than 60 deaths); and turning a light on the monkeys experimented on at Neuralink who advocacy groups say suffered needlessly. Not nearly as adept at all the substantive tasks of running a company as he claims, Elon Musk, Gibney argues, excels mainly at selling tall tales. Even the multiple levels of alleged villainy, however, seem narrow compared to what the director argues is the real game: world domination. In Gibney’s telling, to witness Musk, intentionally or not, convert his satellite internet system, Starlink, into an unelected policymaker given its crucial role in Ukraine and other war-torn places; to see NASA rely so heavily on SpaceX to perpetuate its space program; to watch Musk seemingly use Twitter to garner business favors from world leaders like Modi and Milei; to look with growing dread as the data collected by DOGE potentially becomes a sleeper cell for campaign research and political retaliation — to observe all of this is to gaze upon a man interested not only in wealth and status but in an oligarchal sway that transcends elections’ fickle seasons. Donald Trump may have spent six years bringing the branches of government to heel. But in Gibney’s accounting, Musk is in the process of pulling off something far more menacing: rendering government obsolete altogether. Two revelations, or at least intimations, especially stand out, both involving elections and Musk’s alleged techno- surveilling means of moving them for Republicans. In one, Musk ex and former conservative influencer Ashley St. Clair, a central figure in the documentary, describes the events of Trump’s election in November 2024. Musk, she says, had a “degree of certainty” about the results before they came in that “I had never seen before.” “He had told me [before the election] he was going to unleash the ‘anomaly in the matrix,’ ” she recounts, as a text exchange between them pops up onscreen backing up the claim. We see Musk telling her, “I have ten thousand lasers in space.” “So you think he was referring to Starlink?” Gibney asks off-camera. St. Clair replies, “I mean, I don’t know where else he has space lasers.” Gibney leaves the insinuation hanging — was this a troll or a confession? — but hints he is taking it seriously when he then says in his patented voiceover, “What is Elon building, what are his goals, what are his actual motivations, and do we even know this man at all?” The other piece of the electoral-manipulation insinuation looks not backward but forward and suggests that Musk’s four-month stint in Washington last year did more than gleefully ax 270,000 federal employees and untold billions in life-saving aid (though a section on the latter, anchored by former USAID chief Samantha Power, lands with an outraging wallop). During that time, Gibney suggests, Musk also had access to and potentially collected intimate data on tens of millions of Americans possibly even for later political use. In a follow-up email, Gibney explains further: “We don’t know what DOGE/Musk did with the data to which they had access. What we do know — via my own source who ran IT at a major federal agency and via the whistleblowers and public accounts — is that the DOGE Boys had Super Admin status to federal IT systems. That means they could just slide a copy of the data on all of us to SpaceX as easily as dropping a file into a folder.” (The allegation of salting away data squares with a whistleblower complaint filed by the Social Security Administration’s chief data officer.) “How much data exists in the federal government about every single person living in this country, their voting records, everything that they had ever done?” Wired editor-in-chief Katie Drummond, whose publication led much of this coverage, says in the movie. “Imagine what an AI could do if it can be trained on all that information.” Geoffrey Hinton, the Nobel-prize-winning godfather of AI, offers a specific use case: leveraging the data into an unfair campaign advantage. “It’s fairly clear to me that Trump is hell-bent on corrupting the midterm elections,” he says onscreen. “If you wanted to corrupt those midterm elections and you wanted to use AI, all you needed to do was get detailed information on U.S. citizens. And what DOGE did looked like just what you would do.” Documentarian Alex Gibney, photographed Aug. 20 in Brooklyn, has made a career of exposing abusive power structures, from the U.S. military to Scientology. In Musk, he feels he has found a uniquely dangerous subject: Musk may have left Trump’s side, but what havoc could he wreak, Gibney asks, with the data he surely collected from his short stint atop the so-called Department of Government Efficiency? Photographed by Jake Chessum *** For much of the past 20 years, as television news resources and audiences for longform investigation have waned, documentary filmmakers have risen to take their place. Leading that class has been Gibney. A kind of documentary journeyman, Gibney’s standing changed in the mid-2000s, when, after the age of 50, he directed the eye-opening Oscar nominee Enron: The Smartest Guys in the Room and Taxi to the Dark Side , an intimate, upsetting story of the killing of an Afghan taxi driver by American soldiers during an interrogation. Arriving in George W. Bush’s second term, the film became a focal point for all the frustrations and qualms around the War on Terror. A spate of exposés of other corroded powerful institutions followed as Gibney turned into a kind of investigative journalism gunslinger, coming in to showdown against powerful institutions when few others would. All those films feel like they were leading to this, a point even Gibney will concede. “It’s not the end of the path, but it’s definitely a distillation of the journey,” he says of Musk . As Gibney sits in the edit bay adjusting small details — “Let’s let Trump’s voice go on longer and more distorted so it reads like it’s in Elon’s head,” he says during an Oval Office scene — his worldview comes into focus. Gibney’s tendency is to see the darker side of power and the powerful side of technology, tendencies that cast him as an outlier in the 2010s but have made him more relevant as the years have gone on. In an interview with this reporter about his Stuxnet film Zero Days a decade ago, he outlined hacking threats that seemed exotic, like compromising an American water system. With reports recently about Iranian operatives trying to do just that, they don’t seem so outlandish. “I try to tell a story that opens our eyes and makes us ask the right questions,” he says, speaking of Musk but offering a touchstone that might apply to many of his films. Gibney here has set out to make a movie less about its subject’s history than his future. Sam Harris, the right-leaning podcaster and friend turned enemy of Musk, lays out this theme onscreen near the end of the film. “We are living in a world where one person’s psychopathology and neuropsychological dysregulation is translating into massive consequence in our politics, in our economy, in our geopolitics,” he says. “It’s completely insane we have one person who’s this chaotic — who’s completely unelected — and has this much power.” Gibney makes it clear that he doesn’t think such voices are hyperbolic, and that it is only a certain kind of American heuristic that prevents us from hearing them. “People assume because he’s very rich that he’s not crazy,” he says. “But the terrifying thing might be that he’s crazy and he’s very rich and powerful. That’s the warning bell the film sounds.” The director’s method for ringing that alarm will surely draw debate. Musk did not sit for an interview, going on the offensive at the announcement of the film three years ago by taking to X to call it a “hit piece.” This prompted Gibney, who never met a diss he couldn’t deadpan back, to reply “How would you know?” The line was meant as both undress and challenge, as Gibney at that time still sought an interview. When Musk effectively ended that hope by tweeting, “Gibney is a douche,” Gibney parried back, “Douché,” marking perhaps the first time in human history that a rap battle was settled with an accent aigu. That rejection turned out to be a blessing, birthing dozens of outside sources Gibney turned to instead, on- and off-camera. It also yielded a formal magic trick unexpected in the work of an Oscar-winning documentarian. Gibney and his research team scraped the internet for any audio of Musk they could find. They then created — stick with me here — a video game avatar of Musk speaking those words, Ready Player One -style. The Musk avatar also, in a pair of first-person-shooter sequences, moves through the world as a vintage video game character, complete with health bars and lives left and colorful respawns. “I wouldn’t have gone there if Elon wasn’t so relentless,” Gibney tells me when asked what motivated this choice. “But over and over again in our research, Elon kept coming back to this idea of simulation, how we’re living in an existential video game.” Gibney adds, “We’re playing with levels of reality, and the elements of the Elon Musk story are how he intends to define reality.” (This same wry mischief can be found in the closing credits song, a bouncy original number written and performed by David Byrne that takes jagged pieces of Musk’s own self-mythologizing quotes and slashes him with them.) The effect of Gibney’s digital avatar is surreal, and also its own comment, at once turning Musk into a leather-jacketed larger-than-life character while completely gamifying all his ambitions. The way to neutralize the world’s most powerful man, Gibney believes, is not to cower at his influence but to extend him the same cat-with-a-ball-of-yarn unseriousness he shows us. The move could certainly backfire at a moment when the documentary (and nondocumentary) film world is wary of digital replicas replacing the real thing and AI deepfakes blurring the truth-fiction line. But Gibney says the whimsical device comes in service of a larger truth: the unmasking of a man who has aggregated power only by duping us into thinking we should give it to him. “The Great and Terrible Oz kept people in check because they were afraid of his visage that loomed over everybody, and he used that power to exert an enormous amount of control,” Gibney tells me. “But when a little dog pulled aside the curtain, and you can see a frumpy man operating gears and levers, suddenly he wasn’t so terrible and he wasn’t so great.” “I try to tell a story that opens our eyes and makes us ask the right questions,” notes Gibney, who says he initially admired Musk and proudly owned a Tesla car and solar panel system. Photographed by Jake Chessum *** Gibney presents an intriguing paradox. A Maine resident, he is nonetheless a fixture on New York’s media and entertainment social scene, moving among the kind of powerful people he frequently turns the heat-blaster on. If this has proved conflicting, Gibney does not let on, marching from sacred target to sacred target with little apparent tentativeness. The director has a kind of serious casualness in which he shoulders the weight of the world, but unfussily. Gibney’s is a no-nonsense, bullshit-averse demeanor, which comes out in the editing session when a performative Trump administration ally appears onscreen, prompting an eye-rolling expression with some salty assessments tossed in. For someone who has made a career scalpeling the powerful, it perhaps comes as a surprise that Gibney had never thought of making a documentary about Elon Musk before — and in fact resisted the idea when the Chinese former real estate baron Zhang Xin suggested it to him in 2022 — feeling like so much had been said and, also, wasn’t Musk sometimes a force for good, remaking industries at will? “To be honest, I was on the fence about it,” Gibney says. “But then I talked to a close friend, and he said it was a film about 21st century power, and that resonated with me.” Realizing also that part of his daily life — he was long active on Twitter and had once bought Tesla solar panels — revolved around the mogul, and that no one was really asking questions about what this meant, Gibney sought early financing partners. He found a group of liberal-adjacent production companies ready to work with him, including Anonymous Content ( Navalny ), the upstart doc banner Double Agent (run by an indie film veteran named Dana O’Keefe and joint venture of the narrative film producers Black Bear Pictures and New Regency) and Zhang Xin’s Closer Media. Given the sensitivity of taking on one of the world’s most powerful men (who already viewed the movie as a hit piece), those producers might have expected that they would have to finance the making of the film itself without a sales partner. But when producers took the project out to the market, they were taken aback. Companies that liked to play it safe were willing to take on the far right-flirting Musk. (It was, crucially, before he joined the Trump wagon, but still.) Most notably: Netflix, which pursued a deal despite the streamer avoiding globally polarizing topics like Jamal Khashoggi, surprising even some of the producers. Gibney weighed his options but felt most comfortable with another suitor, HBO’s documentary division, with which he has done some of his most impactful work, including movies about Theranos and Scientology. And so filmmakers in 2023 signed a pact with the platform for U.S. streaming and television rights. In doing so, the parties defied a long-held convention. “Hollywood is either averse to making Elon Musk films because of his politics or afraid of Elon Musk because he could sue,” says Ashlee Vance, the author whose 2015 biography, Elon Musk: Tesla, SpaceX, and the Quest for a Fantastic Future , itself was strangled in development by HBO in 2023 because of what Vance believes were those hesitations. “It makes it that much more surprising this film got through.” (The idea of featuring Elon Musk, of course, has not been anathema in fictional works; as Gibney shows in the film, image-burnishing appearances have cropped up everywhere from Iron Man to The Simpsons to SNL .) Host Elon Musk during the monologue on Saturday Night Live on Saturday, May 8, 2021 Will Heath/NBC/NBCU Photo Bank/Getty Images Then there was the matter of international rights. Most documentaries get sold territory by territory since the interests of countries on a given topic vary, as opposed to one worldwide distributor. This is especially true for a controversial subject — giant global players don’t want a headache because of sensitivities in Croatia. All of which made it unexpected that Universal, one of the biggest international film distributors around, wanted all foreign rights. For the filmmakers, this of course would potentially mean a lot more scrutiny and studio battles than with individual territory buyers. But the idea of making a bigger impact won out. HBO declined to comment about its involvement. This can seem like a strange turn — you can’t put out a movie to tens of millions of people and not want folks to notice — but given Musk’s power and eagerness for a brawl, perhaps logical too. Another entanglement comes in the form of one of the financier-producers. Black Bear is run by Teddy Schwarzman — son of Stephen Schwarzman, the founder of Blackstone and someone who has moved in close circles with Musk, both men part of Trump delegations that met with foreign leaders. (Stephen Schwarzman has called Musk a “fascinating guy” and “good person.”) His son’s willingness to bankroll the most high-profile takedown of Musk in history makes for a potentially interesting Thanksgiving family dinner. Teddy Schwarzman, notably, did not personally take a credit on the film. He did not wish to comment for this piece. HBO’s centrality is especially intriguing. Warner Bros. Discovery, HBO’s parent company, has been run by David Zaslav, a known associate of Musk, the two men prominently sitting together in a luxury box at the U.S. Open two years ago. Gibney’s movie already was well underway. The two even discussed WBD television projects at the match, according to a person familiar with their conversation. But if Musk asked Zaslav to kill the film, the media executive didn’t oblige. Yet huge questions remain given the upcoming changing state of WBD management. Incoming WBD owner Ellison may well run HBO by the time the movie hits the service on an unnamed date in the first half of 2027, and one can’t imagine him feeling too enthused by the onscreen happenings. In addition to the general air of Silicon Valley and Donald Trump skepticism, Ellison’s father and principal financier, Larry Ellison, gets a negative shout-out when he is shown in text messages willing to airdrop Musk $2 billion to buy Twitter, no questions asked. This is not what people pay $111 billion in acquisition fees to platform. Would David Ellison ask for changes? Pull the plug and force producers to self-distribute? (The filmmakers in an unlikely coup retained paid VOD rights.) Gibney and the filmmaking team are holding their breath. So is everyone else. Driven by his interest in colonizing Mars, Musk founded SpaceX in 2002. Dan Tuffs/Getty Images Lost in Space A SpaceX rocket carrying a payload of Starlink satellites, adding to Musk’s already massive fleet — and the power it affords him. Kevin Carter/Getty Images *** How will the movie land with both the public and power brokers? Isaacson’s 2023 book left a lot of reviewers cold with its lack of criticism but still sold a gazillion copies. Gibney’s film could well prove all those book critics right and extend the skepticism to a general public that Musk has to this point kept at bay. The days of An Inconvenient Truth and Fahrenheit 9/11 , in which a documentary becomes an event that moves both box office needles and public sentiment, are well behind us. But is it possible that at this post-Twitter moment, with a need for common vehicles of activism and a new town square, a citizenry this fall will find refuge in Gibney’s movie? It could. Musk’s butchering of the old public commons could deliciously be the reason we make his takedown the new one. The film’s length could paradoxically work in its favor, too, rewarding those who soldier through its four-hour run time with a badge of endurance, not to mention cocktail party cred. “The thing that drives people to theaters is urgency — people feeling that they have to be part of a conversation,” says Kent Sanderson, CEO of Bleecker Street, which is releasing the movie. “And there’s no conversation like the one around someone who affects every single person’s life every single day.” And don’t sleep on the Oscar chattering class. Musk will get a big push for best documentary, and it remains, at this summer vantage point, hard to see what can match it. The biggest X factor, as it were, is how Musk responds. Social media trolls are almost certain, but would he go beyond that? Musk has a history of lashing out legally at those he perceives as harming his interests, filing lawsuits against boycotting Twitter advertisers and his AI rival Sam Altman. The insinuations of business hucksterism are one thing that could provoke him, more intimate details are another. Musk’s personal life comes in for tough scrutiny in the film, with St. Clair’s nauseating details about paternity-based NDA bullying and hush payments (stealth audio from a Musk fixer especially churns the stomach) and her no-comment about his drug use, and with a revealing childhood story Musk’s father tells in which a family friend undergoes a medical emergency while they were all on a road trip in Musk’s native South Africa. The man dies as everyone tries to resuscitate him. Young Elon, his father recounts, reads a comic book, unreactive through the entire episode. Gibney and HBO are insured, and a high-profile group of lawyers has been vigorously stress-testing the film. (Helping matters is that Gibney bases large portions of the documentary on the published work of text journalists from Wired to The Wall Street Journal ; the movie is nothing if not a valedictory for journalism.) Yet that has never stopped a litigious tycoon — especially these days — from going after a media outlet to make a point or extract some concession. Tesla CEO Elon Musk listens as U.S. President Donald Trump speaks to reporters in the Oval Office of the White House on May 30, 2025 in Washington, DC. Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images Alternatively, Musk could learn from the Church of Scientology, which to protest the alleged misrepresentations in Gibney’s 2013 exposé Going Clear took out a full-page ad in The New York Times seeking to debunk the movie. It sent viewership skyrocketing. As Gibney locks in during the editing session, all of that future noise stays outside. More relevant is Musk’s future, as the director tweaks a scene about what the mogul is up to next (humanoid robots and launching himself off a burning planet to Mars). “As he accretes more power, he’s no longer interested in checking his worst impulses,” Gibney says to me, reflecting on Musk’s trajectory. The director pauses, remembering a moment from his reporting. “Someone who worked closely with Elon told me, ‘He’s the most miserable man I’ve ever met.’ So he’s inflicting his misery on everyone else.” The suffering will pile up, Gibney says, until we see what’s behind Toto’s curtain. The Musk Myth How Hollywood burnished the entrepreneur’s image as a benevolent genius. Iron Man 2 (2010) The mere juxtaposition of Musk and Tony Stark implants the idea that the former inspired the latter. The line Musk utters to a passing Robert Downey Jr. (“I have a good idea for an electric jet”) suggests a concept he never had and the reaction of Stark (“Then we’ll make it work”) an easy execution he’s seldom achieved. The Simpsons (2015) Musk arrives in Springfield, where he promptly sets out making alternative energy power plants to help humanity even at the expense of his own profit. Lisa calls him “possibly the greatest living inventor,” and characters regard him as “an intelligence far beyond ours.” The Big Bang Theory (2015) “It feels great to come down here and help the less fortunate,” a real-life Musk tells an awestruck Howard Wolowitz in a soup kitchen on Thanksgiving. Elon Musk, he’s just like us (only more charitable). Rick and Morty (2019) Musk plays an alternate-reality version of himself known as “Elon Tusk,” who joins the title pair in a plan to defeat the evil Heisotron, even polishing his family-man image with a reference to his kids. Saturday Night Live (2021) In inviting Musk (pictured above) to host (over the objections of some castmembers), the show mostly let him good-naturedly clean up his COVID conspiracy theories, give free plugs to DOGEcoin, garner sympathy by discussing his self-reported Aspberger’s and talk about sending people to Mars in a rocket ship as if it’s a real thing. This story appeared in the Sept. 2 issue of The Hollywood Reporter magazine.

title: David Oyelowo & Nate Parker’s Mansa Studios Debuts Slate Of TikTok Microdramas
full_text: Skip to main content By Jesse Whittock Jesse Whittock International TV Co-Editor @WhittockTweets More Stories By Jesse ‘Gunsmoke & Mirrors’, Drama Series About Danish Criminal Turned American Frontier Hero Chris Madsen, In The Works Clíodhna O’Sullivan’s Romantasy Novel ‘Her Hidden Fire’ Getting YA Series Adaptation With Great Island Attached Kevin Hart’s Hartbeat To House Vertical Originals On Microdrama Platform aTwist View All September 2, 2026 6:00am 'I Married the King of the Streets', 'The Love Contract' and 'My Twin Sister Stole My Man' Mansa Studios EXCLUSIVE: David Oyelowo and Nate Parker ‘s Mansa Studios is turning to TikTok for its latest slate of microdramas. The company is launching three vertical shows direct via the TikTok Minis platform. These are My Twin Sister Stole My Man , a relationship-driven drama about betrayal, identity and the complicated ties that bind family together; I Married the King of the Streets, a “high-stakes romance in which love, loyalty and power collide within a dangerous world”; and The Love Contract , which follows a “contract relationship that becomes increasingly complicated when a carefully arranged agreement begins to turn into something real.” Related Stories News Kevin Hart's Hartbeat To House Vertical Originals On Microdrama Platform aTwist News ReelShort Strikes Microdrama Deal With Indonesian Streamer Vidio For 200 Catalogue Titles & Co-Production Of New Shows “Mansa was created to ensure that culturally rich stories can reach audiences wherever they are,” said Oyelowo. “As viewing habits evolve, we are embracing new formats and platforms that allow us to remain connected to our audience while creating meaningful opportunities for diverse storytellers and talent.” Watch on Deadline The launches come following “months of collaboration with TikTok’s team,” according to Mansa’s bosses, and marks the first time Mansa shows have launched on the platform. “TikTok has become the most influential platform in the world for entertainment discovery, making it an ideal home for stories designed to capture audiences immediately and keep them coming back,” said the CAA-repped Parker, co-founder and CEO of Mansa. “Bringing multiple original projects to viewers at once allows us to continue expanding the possibilities of culturally resonant, mobile-first storytelling.” Mansa has been investing in vertical entertainment through 2026. Earlier this year, it announced a slate of 10 original microdrama series spanning romance, drama and other genres. Actor-producers Oyelowo and Parker have turned Mansa as the first microdrama service dedicated to Black stories. It originally launched as an ad-supported streaming platform highlighting Black content for a global audience, and still develops TV and film content alongside microdramas. It also has a theatrical deal with AMC Theatres, which earlier this year gave the long-delayed thriller Newborn a domestic release . Oyelowo, who has been nominated for Golden Globes and Emmys, is know for his role as Martin Luther King Jr. in Selma , while Parker wrote, directed and starred in Sundance favorite The Birth of a Nation . title: George Clooney Tells Venice Studios Are Making Movies That “Need a Launchpad of a Film Festival Less and Less”
full_text: × Skip to main content By Lily Ford Plus Icon Lily Ford @lilyfordtweets Follow Sign Up View All September 2, 2026 5:35am George Clooney at the 2026 Venice Film Festival Courtesy of Getty Naturally, the Venice Film Festival was swiftly fawning over George Clooney on Wednesday, as the Oscar-winning star arrived (via boat, of course) to pick up his Golden Lion Lifetime Achievement Award . Ahead of the glitzy, Jay Kelly -esque honorary ceremony, Clooney sat for a press conference with journalists on the Lido who immediately quizzed him on the Paramount-Warner Bros. merger, the allegations of antisemitism faced by Hollywood peer Mark Ruffalo, and his love of Venice, having gotten married in the Italian city in 2014. Related Stories Movies Slavoj Zizek on Why We Seek Utopias in the Movies (Exclusive Trailer) Movies George Clooney Tackles Paramount-Warner Bros. Merger, Mark Ruffalo, AI and State of U.S. Politics Clooney was also asked about the studio no-show at this year’s film festivals, as well as his directing aspirations. The famed U.S. actor admitted that he hasn’t noticed the studio sit-out at Cannes, Berlin and Venice, which have concentrated their lineups on the best of international cinema. “In fairness, you could make the argument — and this has been going on for 25 or 30 years, this is some of the work that [Steven] Soderbergh and I were doing when we started doing [the 1998 film] Out of Sight and films like that — that studios are doing films that need a launchpad of a film festival less and less,” said Clooney, speaking amid an industry heavily reliant on IP, reboots and franchise projects. “That’s just the nature of the beast,” he continued. “The films that studios are making are hugely expensive, so I think [this situation is] just the fallout from the films they are making, but that’s been going on, literally probably since Jaws , when everything changed… The studios used to make Bonnie and Clyde and All the President’s Men ,” said Clooney. “They don’t really make many films like that [anymore], and so they don’t really need this launchpad as much. I think that would be my only answer to that. I didn’t know that they weren’t really sending that many films over.” Clooney, famed for roles in Ocean’s Eleven , Gravity and Michael Clayton , is also a filmmaker, and even brought his 2005 Good Night, and Good Luck to the festival in 2005. “I’ve had great experiences,” replied the star when probed on whether he’ll be returning to the director’s chair any time soon. “I’ve been nominated for an Oscar, and I’ve also had really bad experiences, and that’s okay,” he laughed. “That’s part of telling stories. I’ve done films that people hated when they came out, and now they like them, and I’ve done films that people liked that [and] now they look at and they think don’t work anymore.” The only reason he is not directing, “is because I have two nine-year-old kids,” said Clooney, who shares twins with Amal. “In order for me to spend time with them, I can’t [direct]. If I act in a movie, it’s three months, and I can go and come and go and come back. When [you] direct a movie, it’s a year, wherever you are, and there’s no traveling back and forth. So I can’t do that anymore. The last thing I did was this play last year on Broadway [the stage adaptation of Good Night, and Good Luck ] and that took us all away for a period of time. And I can’t really pull the kids out of school anymore.” It’s made him “enjoy” being an actor again. “I’m a character actor now.” It was a wide-ranging presser — Clooney, a long-standing advocate for human rights, political activism and climate change awareness — managed to say a few words on how “most of the [world’s] powers that decided climate change is a hoax and science is not real.” He remains an optimist: “That won’t last forever,” though he lamented Europe’s summer battles with wildfires. “We were in Como this summer, and there were fires in Como. It’s been an extraordinarily dry and hot summer, and it’s dangerous.” Clooney confessed that he laughs in response to those who argue climate change is a fad. “Let’s say that everybody who says climate change is bullshit is right,” he began. “The worst thing that could happen by cleaning up the environment is that you create millions more new green jobs, you make the air better to breathe. I mean, there’s no argument against it. That’s the stupidest part of all this. But you know, we’re going to be in it for a while, and then sooner or later we’ll get some governments in there that actually pay more attention to it.” The Venice festival runs Sep. 2-12. THR

title: Netflix Unveils Tense Trailer for ‘East of Eden’ Series Adaptation Starring Florence Pugh
full_text: Skip to main content By Lexy Perez Plus Icon Lexy Perez Senior Digital Editor and Producer View All September 2, 2026 5:30am Florence Pugh as Cathy Ames in episode 103 of Netflix’s ‘East of Eden.’ Courtesy of Netflix Logo text Netflix has released the official trailer for its take on John Steinbeck‘s classic East of Eden . In Zoe Kazan’s adaptation of Steinbeck’s literary masterpiece, Florence Pugh stars as Cathy Ames, whose life is intertwined with with the Trask family, Adam (Christopher Abbott) and Charles (Mike Faist), as they settle in California’s Salinas Valley. Over the years, their paths intersect with the Hamilton family including “Samuel Hamilton (Ciarán Hinds), an Irishman who made his way to California where he raised a family and got to know the land, and Lee (Hoon Lee), a Chinese American whose intellect is surpassed only by his ability to give care to those who need it most, and Faye (Martha Plimpton), a brothel owner whose open heart might lead to her downfall.“ Related Stories Beyond the Book The Adaptation Whisperers: These Producers Are Racing to Find the Next Big Romances TV Matthew Perry Docuseries Set at Netflix In the trailer, tensions are notable with Faist‘s Charles warning Abbott‘s Adam, “A girl like that doesn‘t just fall out of the sky.“ “You need to get rid of her and throw her out. She‘s going to tear you to pieces and I don‘t want to watch it,” Faist‘s Adam later warns. “Evil is not always apparent at first glance. It can come cloaked in goodness or beauty or love. The heart of our oldest stories,“ Pugh is overheard saying in the trailer. The seven-episode limited series , written and executive produced by Kazan, “offers a compelling perspective on the ways in which a family’s history impacts an individual’s present reality.“ Jeb Stuart is also a co-showrunner. Fifth Season and Anonymous Content are producing. The novel was originally adapted for the 1955 film based starring James Dean, Raymond Massey, Richard Davalo, Jo Van Fleet and Julie Harris. Kazan‘s grandfather, Academy Award-winning filmmaker Elia Kazan, directed the film adaptation. “In the process of bringing this family saga to life, the resonance of my own familial connection to the material has not been lost on me,” Kazan said in a statement when the series was announced. “But it is Steinbeck’s writing — personal, shocking, profound and free — that has kept me enthralled to East of Eden since I first read the book as a young teen. Working on this has been the greatest joy, and I am thrilled by the cast and crew we are assembling — and deeply grateful to Netflix, Fifth Season and Anonymous Content for their support.” East of Eden premieres on Netflix on Oct. 1. Watch the trailer below. THR

title: ‘East Of Eden’ Trailer: Evil Lurks “Cloaked In Goodness” In Zoe Kazan’s Limited Series Take On John Steinbeck’s Novel
full_text: Skip to main content By Dessi Gomez , Katie Campione September 2, 2026 5:30am The full trailer for Netflix’s East of Eden limited series adaptation has arrived. Zoe Kazan ’s take on John Steinbeck’s classic 1952 novel will premiere on Netflix October 1. Related Stories News Upcoming Florence Pugh Projects: From ‘East of Eden’ To ‘Dune 3’ Books Everything We Know About Netflix’s ‘East of Eden’ Series So Far “I believe there are monsters born in this world to human parents. A monster is a variation from the accepted normal,” Florence Pugh’s Cathy Ames says in the beginning of the clip. A child may be born perfect, but without kindness or conscience. The show will explore the multigenerational saga of the Trask family, focusing new attention on its indelible antihero, Cathy Ames (Pugh), who shows up to the Trask brothers’ home bloody and crawling, disrupting the brotherhood between Christopher Abbott ’s Adam Trask and Mike Faist ’s Charles Trask, descended from Cyrus Trask (Tracy Letts). Watch on Deadline “Can you tell me your name?” Adam asks her upon her refreshment. “You may call me Cathy,” she replies. Adam thinks Cathy, “brightens the whole house” despite not having left her room much. Charles worries for his brother, claiming “A girl like that doesn’t just fall out of the sky. She’s going to tear you to pieces, and I don’t want to watch it.” L-R: Florence Pugh as Cathy Ames and Christopher Abbott as Adam Trask in ‘East of Eden’ Kirsty Griffin/Netflix Adam proposes marriage to Cathy, promising protection and happiness. “Evil is not always apparent at first glance,” Cathy continues narrating. “It can come cloaked in goodness, or beauty, or love. The heart of our oldest stories.” Here she hints at the ties to the Biblical tale of Cain and Abel, which serves as a framework for East of Eden . The series also stars Martha Plimpton as Faye; Ciarán Hinds as Samuel Hamilton; Joseph Zada as Cal Trask; Joe Anders as Aron Trask and Hoon Lee as Lee. Later on in the trailer, Adam is advised not to leave his and Cathy’s twin boys (Zada and Anders) fatherless when they are already without a mother. L-R: Joe Anders as Aaron Trask and Joseph Zada as Cal Trask in ‘East of Eden’ Courtesy of Netflix “I fear father damned us to the wrong fates,” Faist’s voiceover says, calling back to the boys’ childhood raised by Cyrus. East of Eden hails from co-studios Fifth Season and Anonymous Content. The series was filmed across multiple locations in New Zealand. Kazan wrote the screen adaptation of the novel, which was previously turned into a 1955 movie directed by her grandfather, Elia Kazan. She serves as co-showrunner alongside Jeb Stuart. The two and Pugh executive produce alongside Garth Davis, who directs episodes 1-4; Laure de Clermont-Tonnerre, who directs episodes 5-7; Antoine Douiahy; and Zack Hayden. Nearly four years after the limited series starring Florence Pugh was first announced , Netflix unveiled the first trailer for the seven-episode epic during its upfront presentation on Wednesday, May 13. The series was then teased to launch in fall 2026. Watch the teaser trailer below, and scroll on to find more new photos from the show. title: ‘Dancing With the Stars’ Cast: Jenna Dewan, Julia Stiles, Taylor Hanson and More Join Season 35 — Plus, Which Pros Are Back?
full_text: Sep 2, 2026 5:25am PT ‘Dancing With the Stars’ Cast: Jenna Dewan, Julia Stiles, Taylor Hanson and More Join Season 35 — Plus, Which Pros Are Back? By Emily Longeretta Plus Icon Emily Longeretta 90036 emilylongeretta Latest Inside ‘Married at First Sight’ Season 20: How Peacock’s Changes Led to 1.8 Billion Minutes Viewed, That Wild Reunion and Why Lindsay Hubbard Said No to the Show 6 days ago ‘The Sandlot’ Cast Reunites for ‘Dugout Dads’ Comedy Series, Chris Paul Signs on to Executive Produce 7 days ago Hayden Panettiere, ‘Heroes’ and ‘Scream’ Star, Dies at 36 2 weeks ago See All Michael Buckner “ Dancing With the Stars ” Season 34 set a high bar — and the Season 35 cast is delivering. On Wednesday morning, the celebrity and pro partners were revealed for the Emmy-nominated reality competition, including multiple reality breakout stars, athletes and actors. It also includes Jenna Dewan and Harry Shum Jr., both of whom have extensive dance backgrounds; Dewan began her career as a backup dancer for Janet Jackson, has hosted “World of Dance” and “Flirty Dancing,” and served as a judge on “Come Dance with Me.” Shum Jr. has performed as a backup dancer for Beyoncé, Alicia Keys, Jennifer Lopez and Mariah Carey. On the pro side, last year’s winner, Witney Carson, will return — and dance while pregnant — with Guillermo Rodriguez. title: Slavoj Zizek on Why We Seek Utopias in the Movies (Exclusive Trailer)
full_text: × Skip to main content By Scott Roxborough Plus Icon Scott Roxborough Europe Bureau Chief sroxborough Follow Sign Up View All September 2, 2026 5:00am Slavoj Žižek in Sophie Fiennes' 'The Pervert's Guide to Utopias' Keeper Pictures Slavoj Žižek is back. The Slovenian Marxist philosopher and leftie provocateur, who has become the internet’s most unlikely social media star, returns to cinemas with The Pervert’s Guide to Utopias , the third documentary from director Sophie Fiennes — after The Pervert’s Guide to Cinema (2006) and The Pervert’s Guide to Ideology (2012) — that seeks to filter Žižek’s thinking through the lens of cinema. In her new documentary, which will have its world premiere in Venice on Sept. 7, Fiennes again stages Žižek in re-creations of scenes from the films and TV series being discussed, dropping the philosopher into the cinematic frame, so to speak. He lies in a bathtub in a wedding dress, like Kirsten Dunst, to discusses Lars von Trier’s apocalyptic drama Melancholia (2011). Debates the dystopian vision of Hulu’s A Handmaid’s Tale , lying flat on his back on a bed, draped in a red robe. Related Stories Movies George Clooney Tackles Paramount-Warner Bros. Merger, Mark Ruffalo, AI and State of U.S. Politics Movies Forget the Red Carpet -- Venice's Real Stars Are in the Documentaries This Year Žižek’s hot takes and critical interpretations, on cinema and philosophy, are often counter-intuitive and seemingly contradictory, but never boring. The hidden message behind James McTeigue’s V for Vendetta (2006), he opines in The Pervert’s Guide to Utopias , is not a triumphant one of the masses rebelling against an authoritarian state. Rather the film’s subtext suggest a darker premise: that the fascists need the rebels and the rebels need the fascists to justify each other’s existence. “Our duty is to see things the way they are. And here, cinema helps us,” says Žižek in the first trailer for The Pervert’s Guide to Utopias (see below). “Because I think that the role of Hollywood, or cinema in general, was always to bring out the utopian presuppositions, which we don’t perceive in our ordinary, daily lives. If aliens were to visit our earth, and by chance, ask me, ‘explain us what humanity is about.’ I would not tell them ‘go around and look’ I would tell them ‘look these movies and you will understand us.” The Pervert’s Guide to Utopias is produced by Keeper Pictures, P Guide, SPOK Films, The Film Kitchen, and Mattima Films. Shani Hinto is handling world sales. Check out the exclusive trailer for The Pervert’s Guide to Utopias below. THR

title: Hot Docs Promotes Diana Sanchez, Hires Mara Gourd-Mercado As Festival Seeks To “Future-Proof” Itself
full_text: Skip to main content By Matthew Carey Matthew Carey Documentary Editor, Awards @mattcarey More Stories By Matthew Doc Talk Podcast Goes Live With Director Poh Si Teng And Physicians Of ‘American Doctor’ Watch ‘One In A Million’ Trailer, Oscar Contender That Follows Incredible Journey Of Syrian Girl Across Tumultuous Decade Points North Institute Announces 2026 Artist Programs And Points North Forum Ahead of Camden Film Festival View All September 2, 2026 5:00am Diana Sanchez (left) and Mara Gourd-Mercado Courtesy of Dewey Chang/Oliver Harding Hot Docs , the world-class documentary film festival in Toronto, has announced some major personnel moves – elevating Diana Sanchez to president and bringing in Mara Gourd-Mercado to succeed Sanchez as executive director. Gourd-Mercado, currently head of industry at CPH:DOX in Copenhagen, will report to Sanchez in her new role, which begins October 19. As president, Sanchez will “concentrate on the organization’s strategic direction — artistic oversight, government relations, business development, and major financial partnerships — while safeguarding Hot Docs’ long-term health and stability,” according to a release. Related Stories News Oscar Documentary Contender 'House Of Hope' Secures North American Distribution Documentary West Bank-Set 'House Of Hope,' 'Saigon Story: Two Shootings In The Forest Kingdom' Among Big Winners At Hot Docs The nonprofit Hot Docs, which will celebrate its 34 th edition next year, also announced that Julie Bristow will serve as chair of the organization’s board of directors, while Aaron Zeghers will serve as vice-chair. Watch on Deadline Courtesy of Hot Docs Sanchez tells Deadline the moves are part of “creating a really solid foundation” for Hot Docs, “future-proofing the organization… But the proof will be in the pudding.” In a statement, Bristow, the board chair, praised “the phenomenal work [Sanchez] has done to stabilize and elevate Hot Docs. As we look to the future, this enhanced executive leadership team enables Diana to focus on what matters most: taking Hot Docs to the next level while ensuring it is financially secure, resilient, and nimble.” Just two years ago, before Sanchez’s arrival as executive director, Hot Docs warned it might go under as it faced a financial crisis emerging from the pandemic, a time of enormous challenge for many festivals including Sundance and Montreal’s Just For Laughs. It temporarily shut down its Hot Docs Ted Rogers Cinema and laid off some staff. The 2024 turmoil extended beyond the financial into board governance and artistic operations. Shortly before that year’s festival,10 programmers abruptly left, followed quickly by the resignation of then-Artistic Director Hussain Currimbhoy. Two board members also resigned in the middle of that year’s event. Sanchez says Hot Docs is on the right track, and pointed to a successful 2026 edition, which ran from April 23 to May 3. Mathew Tsang/Getty Images “I think last festival was a real indication, and I think great example of what Hot Docs can deliver,” Sanchez observes. “That’s what I told my team… ‘Let’s just make something great. And then there’ll be word of mouth and people will want to come.’ You can’t do it backwards. You actually have to work on what you’re delivering first, and then that’s when people are going to come back.” To foster stability and growth, she says, “You look at your revenue mix and one of the things I’d like to do is focus on earned revenue, more on that for the coming years. And that’s what I mean by future proofing. It’s like creating these great programs, diversifying our revenue mix, bringing people back by offering something that’s really exciting, being very intentional about what we are actually putting on — ‘You have to live within your means’ kind of thing. So, this year we did the Forum in our cinema, which was great, and people love that experience. And we had a great little delegate lounge close by that was really an intimate space… where people could meet, go and grab coffee. Making it easy for the industry to meet and do business I think is also top of mind.” Hot Docs From her perspective at CPH:DOX, Gourd-Mercado says she saw a renewed appreciation this year for the importance of Hot Docs. “You see the excitement of the people that were there at the [2026] edition. I think that it’s going to only build for the coming editions,” she says, expressing enthusiasm for joining Hot Docs “to participate in building activities and to building a festival where people are going to be excited to go.” As executive director, per the news release, “Gourd-Mercado will lead day-to-day operations and fiscal management of the organization and the festival, including festival and industry fundraising, with an additional focus on industry programming, including a revitalized Hot Docs Forum, and ties with the Francophone doc community in Canada and abroad.” As an Argentinian Canadian and native of Montreal who grew up speaking French, Gourd-Mercado is well situated not only to connect with Canada’s Francophone community, but with documentary makers throughout the Americas as well. “We want to make sure that we are showcasing stories that speak to the moment that we are in now, and that’s globally, not only locally,” notes Gourd-Mercado. “The Americas and Latin America and South America have a lot of great documentary makers. When you look at an event like Conecta in Chile or you look at BAM [Bogotá Audiovisual Market] in Bogotá [Colombia], you can see the incredible amount of projects that are coming out of those regions and those storytellers. And I think it’s our duty as international festivals to also showcase them.” Gourd-Mercado, Sanchez, and Isabel Arrate Fernández – IDFA’s artistic director, who is the child of Chilean political exiles – are among leaders in the documentary festival space who bring international experience and ties to Latin America to their work. “I oversaw Latin American cinema at TIFF for many years. And I was a founding artistic director of the Panama Film Festival,” Sanchez notes. “I also worked with the Los Angeles Latino Film Festival, a wonderful festival as well, every June. There is a very strong tradition of documentary filmmaking from Latin America that’s really informed a lot of my work. And we want to bring in this international experience into Hot Docs as well. We have that kind of vision, which is I think very exciting.” Sanchez’s appointment as Hot Docs president is effective immediately. The 2027 edition of Hot Docs, set for April 23-May 2, is sure to feature a lineup of world premieres and acclaimed documentaries from around the globe. Along with programming a first-class lineup, Sanchez says there’s another dimension to the festival-going experience that she and her colleagues intend to bear in mind. “If you’re a great host, people will also want to come back,” she affirms, “and we’re putting a lot of effort into that.” Baz Bamigboye Looks Back On Tabloid Life With ‘Ink’s Danny Boyle & James Graham Alexander Opens Film Arm With Kevin Chan & Hamish Moseley On Board Tom Cruise Backs WBD Deal & CEO’s Vow Of 30 Pics A Year: “It’s Awesome” Taneo Sebastian Cast In Don Josephus Raphael Eblahan’s ‘Hum’ Read More About: Comments

title: George Clooney Tackles Paramount-Warner Bros. Merger, Mark Ruffalo, AI and State of U.S. Politics
full_text: × Skip to main content By Chris Gardner Plus Icon Chris Gardner chrissgardner Follow Sign Up View All September 2, 2026 4:54am George Clooney is seen during the 83rd Venice International Film Festival on Sept. 2, 2026. (Photo by Victor Boyko/Getty Images) George Clooney touched down on the Lido last year for the world premiere of Noah Baumbach’s Jay Kelly, a film that cast him in the title role as an American actor who travels to Italy to receive a lifetime achievement award only to reflect on the weight of his iconic career and whether it was all worth it. One year later, Clooney, 65, is back at the Venice Film Festival for a spin in the spotlight on the opening night for a bit of life imitating art as he will take the stage inside Sala Grande on Wednesday evening to receive the fest’s highest honor — a Golden Lion for lifetime achievement. As is tradition for such a moment, Clooney braved the international media for an opening day press conference on Wednesday afternoon – and because of who he is and the variety of his art and activism over a 40-plus-year career, he fielded questions on a wide variety of subjects including Hollywood, politics, climate change, the proposed Paramount and Warner Bros. Discovery (WBD) merger, the state of journalism, AI, deep fakes and more. In fact, it’s part of how a democracy works. There are going to be people tonight in the room that are going to disagree with most everything I say or stand for. Fair enough. That’s how it’s supposed to be. We’re supposed to argue these things out and come to a conclusion based on the information that we take in.” He continued: “I will always support Mark Ruffalo’s ability to speak freely. I like him. He’s a good man.” As for the merger itself, Clooney called it a “complicated thing” that he doesn’t quite foresee going through or benefiting the deal architects like David Ellison. “I don’t know how this goes through. There are so many issues involved,” he said. “It doesn’t matter how much money you have; it’s going to be very tricky to do. We’re not on taking the lead on it.” As for how AI impacts him personally, Clooney quipped, “Well, I would like to avoid being in a tampon commercial 20 years after I’m dead. I would like to avoid that.” Artistic director Alberto Barbera and Clooney on Sept. 2, 2026.
