It was that way in the 1700s. It is that way now. It’s a concern for a moment, but I do believe that information will find its way out.” That said, he called it “a concern” that “the richest people in the world right now are owning the Washington Post and [Twitter aka X], most of the places we get our information,” referencing Jeff Bezos and Elon Musk, respectively. “I think five or six of the biggest outlets for information are owned by the richest people in the world. That’s a concern, but there’s still a lot of room for good journalism.” He was also asked to reflect on the art imitating life piece of it all with Jay Kelly and whether today feels like his arc in the film, which was described as “romantic but also melancholy.” “It’s a little bit similar to the tribute I get in the movie, which is kind of funny. You know, I’m 65 years old; everything is melancholy. Literally, you brush your teeth, and you’re like, oh, my teeth used to be so much nicer. Everything about getting older, you get a little melancholy,” he explained. “I also feel very lucky. I have an incredible wife who I love very much and loves me, and I have great kids … I continue to be able to work when I want to. You know, life is pretty good.” Clooney continued by saying that while he’s in a good place, there’s a lot of stuff in the world that isn’t. While that takes a lot of focus at times, as it should, “we also have to remember to celebrate the good things that are happening in our lives.” One good thing that’s about to happen in his life is reteaming with close friends like Brad Pitt and Matt Damon in another Ocean’s Eleven installment. Clooney teased that project, which has already been announced by saying, “We have an Ocean’s film that we’re going to shoot as soon as we get our schedules worked.” Clooney is just about as beloved as they come here in Venice. The actor has a long history with the festival both as an actor and filmmaker dating back several decades to the world premiere of Steven Soderbergh’s 1998 drama Out of Sight opposite Jennifer Lopez. His history also includes the Coen brothers’ film Intolerable Cruelty opposite Catherine Zeta-Jones, the Clooney-directed Good Night and Good Luck , Tony Gilroy’s Michael Clayton , another Coen effort, Burn After Reading with Brad Pitt, another Clooney special with The Ides of March , Alfonso Cuarón’s Gravity co-starring Sandra Bullock, Clooney’s Suburbicon , and more recently with Jon Watts’ Wolfs , also opposite Pitt. But he’s also treated as a sort of countrywide hero as well thanks to his longtime residency of Lake Como with wife, Amal Clooney and their twins. Amal has accompanied him to this year’s festival. She got a lot of attention from the podium from Clooney today. “I will say I have had a love story with Venice for about 30 years, and in fact was married here, and so I would say that my greatest moment here was obviously my wedding because I would get in a lot of trouble if I don’t say that,” he quipped. But he spread the love to the festival as well. “This is a film festival that has been very dear to me. My first big directing gig was Good Night, and Good Luck. I’ve had immense successes and I’ve had massive failures. I remember I was here with Catherine Zeta-Jones for Intolerable Cruelty , and none of the jokes played here, and it was over. Usually, people stand up and applaud, and everybody just turned and looked at us. I looked at Catherine and I said, ‘Run!’ And we ran out of the theater.” But there have been plenty of “wonderful” moments as well. “Careers are really funny. It’s so many different accidents that get you here, so many different lefts and rights, and things that could have gone wrong or right. It’s hard to sustain all of that, and you have to rely on kindness of friends and kindness of people you work with,” he said. “But it really requires luck all the way through.” Clooney signs autographs at the close of the 62nd Venice Film Festival on Sept. 10, 2005. title: Forget the Red Carpet — Venice’s Real Stars Are in the Documentaries This Year
full_text: × Skip to main content By Patrick Brzeski Plus Icon Patrick Brzeski Asia Bureau Chief View All September 2, 2026 4:00am 'Oasis: Dont Look Back in Anger' Courtesy of Venice Some of the biggest stars at this year’s Venice Film Festival won’t be the famous faces walking the red carpet, but the wildly high-profile subjects of documentaries that range from intoxicating to grippingly urgent. From Oscar winner Alex Gibney ‘s 4-hour dissection of Elon Musk and Disney’s intimate Oasis reunion movie to NAZA , the politically charged documentary about “Israel’s calculated mass killing of Palestinian civilians in Gaza,” and the ICE documentary They’re Here from Laura Poitras (another Oscar winner) — many of this year’s must-see movies on the Lido are clearly nonfiction. And, arguably, the biggest star who may or may not walk Venice’s red carpet — aside from Noel and Liam Gallagher — will likely do so on behalf of a documentary. Noted architecture superfan Brad Pitt recently became an executive producer of Wim Wenders’ 14-year-in-the-making documentary portrait of Peter Zumthor, the Swiss visionary behind the sprawling new Los Angeles County Museum of Art — another gem among Venice’s stacked 2026 documentary lineup. “It’s a phenomenal year for docs at Venice, and I think this will be one of the big stories of this edition,” says Emilie Spiegel, who co-heads Cinetic Marketing, a prestige publicity agency that represents an outsized swath of every fall’s awards favorites. “To have the oldest festival in the world so clearly state that documentary is cinema, and that some of the most exciting work is happening there, is really significant. Amid budget contractions and studio consolidation, I also think it’s optimistic and savvy of Venice to be championing nonfiction right now.” For breadth, depth, diversity and pedigree, Venice has clearly emerged as the preeminent platform for high-end nonfiction filmmaking among the world’s top festivals. While Cannes has been far more sporadic in its support of the form, and Berlin tends to offer quantity at the expense of quality, Venice has consistently brought the bangers — and the 2026 selection looks to be among its best yet. Two-time Oscar winner Barbara Kopple is back with Union Town , a cinéma vérité portrait of New York delivery workers taking on some of the world’s most powerful corporations; Free Solo Oscar winners Jimmy Chin and Elizabeth Chai Vasarhelyi return to extreme sporting terrain with Everest: The Other Side , about a pair of mountaineers’ audacious attempt to climb and ski the north face of the world’s tallest mountain; The Truffle Hunters duo Michael Dweck and Gregory Kershaw decamp to French wine country for an infectiously romantic and richly informative romp in Burgundy ; and Takashi Miike, after more than 100 films and three decades spent gleefully jumping around genres, makes his first documentary with Shumei: The Living Legacy of Kabuki , filmed over more than three years with rare access to the inner sanctum of Japan’s traditional Kabuki theater world. Related Stories Movies Maggie Gyllenhaal Takes on Venice Film Festival's Lack of Women in Competition: "There's a Systemic Problem" Movies A Family and Country Are in Crisis in 'Our Share of Sand' (Exclusive Venice Clip) ‘Musk,’ courtesy of Venice Film Festival Courtesy of the Venice Film Festival Elsewhere, Julia Loktev follows her epic portrait of independent Russian journalists with My Undesirable Friends: Part II – Exile , another nearly six-hour immersion; Russell Crowe turns the camera on himself and his globe-trotting rock band for what Venice chief Alberto Barbera has called the star’s “most personal” film. And that’s before factoring in Erik Shirai’s Sumo: Spirit Weighs Nothing , which promises rare access inside another of Japan’s most famously guarded traditions; Robert Greene’s Too Much Sugar , a strikingly original doc about fatherhood and masculinity; Mariano Llinás’ more-than-five-hour biography of Jorge Luis Borges; or two-time Oscar-shortlisted director Victor Kossakovsky’s radical examination of the life of trees, Holy Wood Dust. The festival has even built its embrace of docs more firmly into its structure this year, with a new dedicated “Film on Films” strand, where Luca Guadagnino’s gargantuan, seven-hour-plus meditation on the great Bernardo Bertolucci sits alongside Sophie Fiennes and Slavoj Zizek’s The Pervert’s Guide to Utopias, a tribute to the cult of Seijun Suzuki, and more. Documentary filmmaking’s presence at Venice stretches back to the festival’s very first edition in 1932, when Joris Ivens and Mannus Franken’s 12-minute Dutch avant-garde documentary Rain (or Regen ) screened on the closing night of the inaugural edition. But it wasn’t until the Barbera era that nonfiction filmmaking would vie for — and swiftly win — the festival’s signature honor. Shortly after taking the reins as artistic director of the festival for the second time in 2012, Barbera put two documentaries in the festival’s main competition for the first time in 2013 — Errol Morris’ The Unknown Known and Gianfranco Rosi’s Sacro GRA — and the latter promptly won the Golden Lion. The space and prominence Barbera has accorded to nonfiction has only grown in the years since. “Perhaps this is not the result of a deliberate strategic choice, but rather the consequence of the fact that, year after year, we receive a growing number of submissions in the documentary genre, whose significance — both from an aesthetic standpoint and in terms of its ability to offer a representation of and contribute to our understanding of the major issues of our time — is perhaps unprecedented,” Barbera explains. “My impression is that the financial resources available for making documentaries have increased, as a result of growing demand from streaming platforms but also increased interest from the public, which is now much more willing to watch nonfiction films of good quality.” ‘From Inside Out: The Architecture of Peter Zumthor,’ courtesy of Venice Film Festival Road Movies In docs as well as fictional filmmaking, Venice has also staked out a commendably independent-minded stance over recent years when it comes to films that tackle conflict and fraught social issues. “I believe Venice is one of the very few international cultural platforms that has the ability to invite filmmakers with very different — or even opposite — political positions and cultural points of view, and put their work in conversation,” says Ukrainian director and producer Alexander Rodnyansky, who is known for his work with Russian auteur Andrey Zvyagintsev and last year directed and premiered the searingly personal documentary Notes from a True Criminal in Venice. Rodnyansky notes the sober-mindedness Venice has shown in screening bold Ukrainian and Palestinian films — such as The Voice of Hind Rajab in 2025 and the Gaza docs NAZA and Ahmed Hassouna’s Citizen Osama this year — as well as works by freethinking Russian and Israeli filmmakers, without succumbing to the blanket bans that some have called for on films and filmmakers from those countries. “Of course, state propaganda should have no place, but real independent-minded filmmaking should be welcomed wherever it comes from,” he says. Rodnyansky is producer of Israeli documentarian Amos Gitai’s The Road to Jericho , a journey from Jerusalem to Jericho that visits the country’s threatened Bedouin community while reflecting on the Israeli-Palestinian peace process. The film will premiere in Venice’s out-of-competition nonfiction section. “As you understand, it’s not an easy time for Israeli filmmakers right now. They’re having a very hard time getting their movies accepted by the major festivals, regardless of what they might believe,” Rodnyansky says. “These are turbulent times, and a festival should try to reflect the polarization of the societies we observe and continue the conversation using artistic means,” he adds. “It’s a very simple mission, and I think Barbera inherited that legacy and has continued to enrich it in a brilliant way.” THR

title: Maggie Gyllenhaal Takes on Venice Film Festival’s Lack of Women in Competition: “There’s a Systemic Problem”
full_text: × Skip to main content By Patrick Brzeski Plus Icon Patrick Brzeski Asia Bureau Chief View All September 2, 2026 3:51am Maggie Gyllenhall at Venice 2026 Courtesy of Tiziana Fabi/AFP via Getty Images Politics and the underrepresentation of women at the world’s major film festivals became the breakout topic of conversation at this year’s Venice jury press conference, with Maggie Gyllenhaal stating that she believes “there’s a systemic problem” behind the fact that the world’s oldest cinema showcase has just two titles directed by women in its main competition this year. “It’s much harder for women to get their films financed,” said Gyllenhaal, the festival’s competition jury president this year, when asked about the dearth of women in Venice’s selection. “Also, could it be possible that the things that women, having had a different experience of being alive in the world, want to make movies about are not always deemed high art?” Related Stories Movies A Family and Country Are in Crisis in 'Our Share of Sand' (Exclusive Venice Clip) Movies Brad Bird's 'Ray Gunn,' Travis Knight's 'Wildwood' Among BFI London Film Fest World Premieres “I really am walking in with a question as to why there are so few women in the main competition,” she later added. This year’s competition has drawn scrutiny for its stark gender imbalance. Just one of the original list of 20 Golden Lion contenders — May el-Toukhy’s Woman Unknown — is directed by a woman, down from six female-directed competition titles last year. The festival later added to the competition with the Gaza documentary NAZA , co-directed by Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor, bringing the total to two. Venice artistic director Alberto Barbera acknowledged the disparity when announcing the lineup, calling it a recent low for the festival. But Gyllenhaal also tipped her hat to Venice for selecting her as the event’s jury chief this year. “Alberto and Julia asking me to be the head of the main jury competition — after the two films in particular that I have made — is a very important thing to consider, too,” she said. Gyllenhaal’s jury includes Tunisian filmmaker Kaouther Ben Hania, whose acclaimed Palestinian drama The Voice of Hind Rajab won last year’s Silver Lion Grand Jury Prize; Oscar-winning composer Daniel Blumberg; film scholar Francesco Casetti; French director Xavier Giannoli; Afghan filmmaker Shahrbanoo Sadat; and Hong Kong filmmaking legend Johnnie To. Together they will select the Golden Lion winner and Venice’s other main competition prizes from a field that includes Danny Boyle’s Rupert Murdoch drama Ink , Robert Pattinson thriller Primetime , Martin McDonagh’s Wild Horse Nine , Korean auteur Lee Chang-dong’s much-anticipated return Possible Love and NAZA , among others. Gyllenhaal has a significant history with Venice. Her 2021 feature directing debut, The Lost Daughter , premiered in competition on the Lido and earned her the festival’s best screenplay prize before going on to receive three Oscar nominations. She also has a project in Venice this year. Her Marilyn Monroe-inspired advertorial short Flesh Impact , starring Dakota Johnson, Ellen Burstyn and Peter Sarsgaard, will screen out of competition later in the event. The press conference proceeded after some confusion during the weekend over whether the jury’s meeting with the media — a staple of all major film festivals — would take place at all. Venice organizers stated on Saturday that the jury presser might be scrapped due to a “scheduling conflict” involving a jury member; but by Sunday, the festival said a solution had been found, and the briefing would be held as usual. The brief interregnum stirred industry speculation about the role politics might play at the 83rd edition, as various global conflicts — the war in Gaza, Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, and the U.S.-Iran war — loom in the background of the world’s oldest film festival. Festival chief Barbera has described this year’s lineup as the “most political” of recent years. Venice’s blue-chip festival peers, meanwhile, showed earlier this year the two directions a major cultural event might take amid this globally fraught moment. In February, the Berlin festival became engulfed by political discord and social media point-scoring after jury president Wim Wenders told reporters during the opening press conference that filmmakers “have to stay out of politics.” But the Cannes Film Festival later went ahead in May with plenty of carefully calibrated political statements from filmmakers but notably less acrimony. Gyllenhaal was asked near the outset of the Venice press conference whether she feels filmmakers have a responsibility to be political amid the world’s current challenges. “We could say, ‘How are we possibly here talking about movies right now, when the world is in a state of emergency?'” she replied. “To me, the answer has something to do with empathy. I think that film allows an opening into an opportunity to find empathy inside of ourselves. Personally, I don’t believe that there is any subject or any filmmaker that shouldn’t be heard. I think we can challenge ourselves to hear stories about the most corrupt, the most perverse people, because it opens up the opportunity to find empathy for those people — and even to look at the ways in which we might have a little bad guy inside us, a little perversity inside us, a little corruption inside us, fight it as we might.” She added: “I think that if movies really are an honest look into other people’s experience, then they are fundamentally, unavoidably political, as well as a lot of other things.” The 83rd edition of the Venice Film Festival officially opens Wednesday evening on the Lido with a ceremony that will fete George Clooney with a Golden Lion for lifetime achievement and conclude with the world premiere of Boyle’s Ink , starring Jack O’Connell, Guy Pearce, and Claire Foy. The festival concludes with an awards ceremony on Sept. 12. THR

title: Venice Jury President Maggie Gyllenhaal Says Films Are ‘Fundamentally, Unavoidably Political’ and Questions Lack of Female Directors in Competition: ‘There’s a Systemic Problem’
full_text: Sep 2, 2026 3:49am PT Venice Jury President Maggie Gyllenhaal Says Films Are ‘Fundamentally, Unavoidably Political’ and Questions Lack of Female Directors in Competition: ‘There’s a Systemic Problem’ By Elsa Keslassy , Rebecca Rubin It didn’t take long for politics to take the spotlight at this year’s Venice Film Festival jury press conference. Amid the wars raging in Gaza and Ukraine, as well as the unrest in the United States, jury president Maggie Gyllenhaal was asked whether cinema should be political. “OK,” Gyllenhaal said with a laugh. “May as well get into it.” The filmmaker of “The Bride” and “The Lost Daughter” directly addressed the question by sharing her belief that movies are “fundamentally, unavoidably political.” Related Stories 'Godzilla Minus Zero' Named Centerpiece of Tokyo Film Festival as 'Sukiyaki' Opens, 'Colony' Closes Kaskade, Electronic Music Icon, Signs With Pacific Music Group in Asia Partnership (EXCLUSIVE) “Look, we could say, how are we possibly here talking about movies right now when the world is in a state of emergency?” she said. “To me, the answer has something to do with empathy. I am here curious.” Gyllenhaal was also probed about the lack of female directors in this year’s competition lineup. Only one film up for the Golden Lion — the drama “Woman Unknown” by Danish-Egyptian director May El-Toukhysolely — was solely directed by a women. “I guess it’s finally become clear that men make better movies than women do,” Gyllenhaal deadpanned. Venice artistic director Alberto Barbera interjected, saying that “Naza,” a documentary co-directed by “No Other Land” filmmakers Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor, was added to the competition lineup shortly before the festival. Gyllenhall returned to the question, saying, “I will answer you seriously. There’s a systemic problem. It’s harder for women to get films financed.” She wondered aloud: “Could it be possible that women, having had a different experience of being alive in the world, want to make movies about are not always deemed high art? Who decide what’s good? Who decides what is valuable?” Gyllenhall also noted it was significant that she was chosen to be head of the main competition jury. She’s presiding over a seven-member committee that includes Tunisian helmer Kaouther Ben Hania, Hong Kong filmmaker Johnnie To, Afghan director Shahrbanoo Sadat, French filmmaker Xavier Giannoli, British composer Daniel Blumberg and Italian film scholar Francesco Casetti. Gyllenhaal represented the jury at the conference, while her fellow members sat in the audience. The traditional opening jury press conference took place after some uncertainty over whether Venice would hold it at all. The festival considered scrapping the event because of “scheduling issues,” which some perceived as a way to shield jury members from being quizzed about politics. After facing backlash, the festival reinstated the jury presser, explaining the programming conflicts had been solved. The debate surrounding the press conference came amid heightened political tensions on the international festival circuit, where actors, directors and jury members have increasingly been pressed to address wars, Gaza, U.S. politics and the rise of the far right. The conversation around politics escalated at the Berlin Film Festival earlier this year after jury president Wim Wenders said filmmakers should “stay out of politics” while fielding questions about Israel and Palestine. His remarks triggered fierce criticism and prompted Berlin artistic director Tricia Tuttle to publicly defend artists’ right to decide whether or not to speak on political issues. Venice is opening against a particularly charged backdrop. An open letter issued by the Venice4Palestine collective and signed by figures including Nobel Prize-winning writer Annie Ernaux, Roger Waters, Isabel Coixet and Matteo Garrone has called on the festival to take “concrete action” in support of Palestine. The group has also asked Venice to fly the Palestinian flag throughout the festival. The subject carries particular resonance for Ben Hania, whose Gaza drama “The Voice of Hind Rajab” premiered in competition at Venice last year and won the Silver Lion after receiving a 22-minute standing ovation. Barbera has himself described this year’s selection as the festival’s most political in recent years, pointing to films dealing with war, Palestine, immigration, climate change, mounting social tensions and shrinking freedoms. “We are a space for freedom of expression,” Barbera told Variety prior to the start of the festival . “Our role is to safeguard freedom of expression for everyone, for the artists, and to safeguard the confrontation between artists and the public, the critics and people in general.” ‘NAZA’ Documentary From ‘No Other Land’ Directors Acquired by MK2 Films Ahead of Venice Film Festival Premiere George Clooney Defends Mark Ruffalo’s ‘Ability to Speak Freely’ About Paramount-Warner Bros. full_text: Sep 2, 2026 3:44am PT Ruben Östlund’s Plattform Produktion Boards Jessica Hausner’s Satirical Drama ‘Toxic’ Ahead of Venice Gap-Financing Market (EXCLUSIVE) The Swedish label joins Austria's Schubert, Germany's Essential Films and France's Société Parisienne de Production in the pan-European co-production By Christopher Vourlias Plus Icon Christopher Vourlias Latest Ruben Östlund’s Plattform Produktion Boards Jessica Hausner’s Satirical Drama ‘Toxic’ Ahead of Venice Gap-Financing Market (EXCLUSIVE) 3 hours ago Austrian Director Sandra Wollner’s ‘Everytime’ Wins Best Film at Sarajevo Film Festival 2 weeks ago ‘Supporting Role’ Director Ana Urushadze Preps ‘Fear of Butterflies,’ a Detective Story With ‘Mysticism and a Touch of Body Horror’ (EXCLUSIVE) 2 weeks ago See All Courtesy of Barbara Seyr Ruben Östlund ’s Plattform Produktion has joined “Toxic,” the forthcoming satirical workplace drama from “Club Zero” director Jessica Hausner , which is among the projects being pitched during the Venice Gap-Financing Market taking place Sept. 4 – 6. The pan-European co-production is produced by Schubert (Austria), Essential Films (Germany), Société Parisienne de Production (France) and Plattform Produktion (Sweden). Related Stories 'VIII: Awakening' Wraps Production in Beijing, Marking KC Global Media Asia's First China Original (EXCLUSIVE) 'Wildwood' and 'Ray Gunn' to World Premiere at London Film Festival as 'Ink,' 'Club Kid,' 'Bunker,' 'La Bola Negra,' 'Wild Horse Nine' and More Join Lineup Told across four chapters, “Toxic” explores different aspects of the modern world of work. Through contemporary parables, it follows employees and employers within a capitalist system on the verge of outpacing itself. With a tone at times realistic, at others more absurd, it’s tied together by the human element that acts as the sand in the gears of a profit-driven world. Popular on Variety Working off a script co-written by Jessica Lind, Hausner said she was interested in exploring the many contradictions of capitalism, and the “mutual dependency” between workers and employers that’s fostering ever-growing economic gaps while leaving so many unfulfilled. “Is this system we work and live in the best system we can come up with?” she asked. The question cuts to the very heart of a modern condition in which “our identities and the respect we command are often defined by our job and pay grade,” she said. “Meaning in life is really created through the ideology of our society. As an individual, I don’t think one can find meaning all alone,” she said. “Meaning is created through others — through the eyes of my fellows in society. It is very much a question bound to the system we work in.” Through its parallel storylines, the film explores how our understanding of self-realization in the workplace is evolving, contrasting exploitation and overwork with our desire to find meaning in our professional lives. Set within four different workplaces — an advertising agency; a waste disposal company; a nursing home; and an unprofitable retail chain — it examines how deeply people have internalized performance-driven pressures, and asks whether change is possible within a system rooted in profit and success. Hausner’s last film, “Club Zero,” was set at a British boarding school where a nutrition teacher — played by Mia Wasikowska — pushed a gospel of mindful abstinence on her students, transforming them into a cult. In a glowing review out of Cannes, Variety ’s Owen Gleiberman praised the “gripping and provocative” film as an “audaciously disturbing drama.” Speaking to Variety from her home in Vienna, Hausner explained how “Toxic” is in conversation with her previous films. “What is satisfying? What is it that really makes a life worth living? In my films, I always try to circle around these questions,” she said. “Not only on an individual level. I’m always interested in the societal level. Why am I made to think or to believe something? This is what I try to focus on in all my films. The way we are being manipulated, in a subtle, everyday-like way, by the society we live in.” But what happens when society is in flux? Across Europe, the director noted, governments are mulling whether the continent’s work-life balance needs to be reconsidered. “The social system is becoming less affordable. This is an economic problem,” she said. “Many countries in Europe have to shift their social expenses from social care into building more weapons.” Meanwhile, inequality is growing, and work itself, as Hausner put it, “no longer pays off, neither financially nor in terms of fulfilment.” As “Toxic” illustrates, that leaves societies with many difficult questions and no easy answers — least of all from the tech barons and free-market evangelists who push capitalism as the miracle cure to all that ails us. “If we knew a better solution, we would probably already be heading there,” said Hausner. “But it’s not at all obvious what the next step is.” Venice-Selected ‘Agata the Writer,’ Starring Mia Wasikowska, Boarded by MMM Film Sales (EXCLUSIVE) Chinese Feature ‘Big Little Things’ Turns a Real-Life Family Rift Into a Coming-Out Drama Now Headed for Venice Horizons (EXCLUSIVE) Ruben Östlund’s Plattform Produktion Boards Jessica Hausner’s Satirical Drama ‘Toxic’ Ahead of Venice Gap-Financing Market (EXCLUSIVE) Venice: M-Appeal Picks Up Chinese Director Jie Dong’s ‘Zoom In, Zoom Out’ Ahead of Premiere (EXCLUSIVE) Who’s Afraid of Film Festivals? He follows in the footsteps of Fanny Herrero ( Call My Agent! ), who received last year’s French TV Disruptor Award. The award will be presented to Zag at the closing cocktail reception at the Rendez-Vous, which is a glitzy affair held at the historic Montivilliers Abbey and hosted by Hervé Morin, President of the Normandy Region. The French TV Disruptor Award is in recognition of Zag’s contribution to the world of TV. title: ‘Kill Jackie’: Catherine Zeta-Jones Is On The Run In Prime Video & AMC+’s Pulsating Thriller Series; Launch Date Set
full_text: Skip to main content By Jesse Whittock Jesse Whittock International TV Co-Editor @WhittockTweets More Stories By Jesse David Oyelowo & Nate Parker’s Mansa Studios Debuts Slate Of TikTok Microdramas ‘Kill Jackie’: Catherine Zeta-Jones Is On The Run In Prime Video & AMC+’s Pulsating Thriller Series; Launch Date Set ‘Gunsmoke & Mirrors’, Drama Series About Danish Criminal Turned American Frontier Hero Chris Madsen, In The Works View All September 2, 2026 3:00am Buckle up for a global thrill ride. Catherine Zeta-Jones is on the run in the first trailer for action series Kill Jackie . Zeta-Jones is is seen shooting shotguns, taking out home-raiding assassins with guns hidden in artwork and charting a private aircraft as her character, former drug smuggler Jackie Price, attempts to evade The Seven Demons, a squad of the world’s most terrifying hired hitmen. There’s even a nod to 28 Days Later , with Zeta-Jones hobbling across a deserted Westminster Bridge in London wearing blue hospital scrubs, just like Cillian Murphy’s Jim in the 2002 horror movie. Watch the full trailer above. Related Stories Casting Alex Kingston, Iain Glen & Sean Pertwee Among 7 Cast In Prime Video's Ray Winstone Action-Comedy Series 'Danger Money' News Prime Video Sets Premiere Date For Third & Final Season Of 'Maxton Hall' The trailer comes as distributor Fremantle revealed that Stan in Australia, Yes in Israel, Sky TV in New Zealand, Sky Italia in Italy and Globoplay in Brazil have acquired the show. Prime Video was the orginal buyer, taking it for the UK, Ireland, Netherlands, Turkey, Germany, Austria, Switzerland, Liechtenstein, Luxembourg and Canada, with AMC+ snapping up U.S. rights. Watch on Deadline In further news, Prime Video, AMC+ and Stan have announced a October premiere date with the other territories announcing soon. Based on Sunday Times bestselling author Nick Harkaway ‘s acclaimed novel The Price You Pay , the eight-part series follows Zeta-Jones as Jackie Price, a former international drug smuggler whose carefully constructed new life is thrown into chaos when a team of elite assassins is sent to kill her. The show comes from creative talent behind Killing Eve and Gangs of London , and stars Zeta-Jones ( Chicago , Wednesday ) alongside Daniel Ings ( A Knight of the Seven Kingdoms, The Gentlemen ), Sidse Babett Knudsen ( Prime Target , Borgen ), Bill Paterson ( Fleabag , Criminal Justice ), Ron Perlman ( Hellboy ), Óscar Jaenada ( Rambo V , Cantinflas ) and Hattie Hook ( Of An Age , Ten Pound Poms ) among others. Also cast are Darci Shaw ( A Thousand Blows , This City is Ours ), Raff Law ( Masters of The Air , Triton ), Enzo Cilenti ( Black Mirror , The Crown ), Christine Adams ( Hijack , Malice ), Julian Rhind-Tutt ( Britannia , Napoleon ), Karlis Arnolds Avots ( Soviet Jeans , Lovable ), Set Sjöstrand ( The Wheel of Time , Valhalla ), Tadashi Ito ( Society of the Snow , The Platform 2 ), Sebastian Armesto ( Gangs of London , A Small Light ), Julian Barratt ( The Mighty Boosh , The Great ), Gavin Spokes ( House of The Dragon , Slow Horses ), Jonathan Cake ( And Just Like That , Camping ) and Bamshad Abedi-Amin ( A Town Called Malice , The Last Kingdom ). Fremantle and Steel Springs Pictures are the co-producers, with Conor Keane, Tom Butterworth ( Gangs of London ), Peter Lawson ( John Wick ) and Damon Thomas ( Killing Eve ) the co-creators. Butterworth is the writer and showrunner and Keane co-wrote the TV adaptation and is an associate producer. Harkaway was an executive consultant. Executive producers are Lawson and Jose Agustin Valdes for Steel Springs, Butterworth, Damon Thomas, Zeta-Jones, Rebecca Dundon, Dante Di Loreto and Jeffrey Levine. The lead director is Damon Thomas. title: Baz Bamigboye Looks Back On True Tabloid Life With ‘Ink’ Director Danny Boyle & Writer James Graham – Venice Film Festival
full_text: Skip to main content By Baz Bamigboye Baz Bamigboye Columnist/International Editor At Large @BazBam More Stories By Baz Breaking Baz: Broadway’s Intoxicating ‘Buena Vista Social Club’ Musical Eyes London Transfer In 2027, Say Producers Orin Wolf & Barbara Broccoli Breaking Baz: ‘MobLand’s Joanne Froggatt In Advanced Talks To Play Quaker Leader In MGM+’s ‘The Magnificent Seven’ Remake Breaking Baz: Hammer’s ‘Horror Of Dracula’ Starring Christopher Lee Is Ready To Sink Its Teeth Into Audiences At Halloween With Censored Scenes Restored – Exclusive Interview View All September 2, 2026 3:00am (L to R) Guy Pearce as Murdoch and Jack OConnell as Lamb in Ink. Anthony Dickenson The Sun sure shone for me. “Get on the bloody Concorde with Jerry!” The Sun’s news editor barked when I rang in the old-fashioned way from a call box at JFK. It was 1982. When I queried how to pay for the hefty cost of a seat on an Air France supersonic jet to Charles de Gaulle airport in Paris, I was told, “Pick up the pre-paid ticket from the desk and get on the bloody plane.” The ‘Jerry’ in question was Jerry Hall. She was dating Mick Jagger but had entered into a brief fling with racing tycoon Robert Sangster, who was a big noise back then. Related Stories Festivals Zurich Bolsters Position As Awards Circuit Stop-Off As 'Bunker', 'Club Kid' & 'Adult Supervision' Join Gala Lineup News Guy Pearce Gives 'Priscilla, Queen Of The Desert 2' Filming Update My Sun colleagues back at the paper’s Fleet Street office had just discovered that Jagger was planning to reunite with Hall, the glamorous cover girl and catwalk star, in Paris. My task was to accompany her on the flight and get her to talk. Even a simple “hello” or “piss off” from her was worth a thousand words to the paper. Watch on Deadline John Kay, The Sun’s then-chief reporter, used to say that whatever words a subject uttered was copy. You could, in theory, write, ”Jerry Hall spoke for the first time today, amid her reunion with Rolling Stones front man Mick Jagger, following her brief liaison with millionaire playboy Robert Sangster…” And that’s how it went down. Legendary photographer Arthur Edwards was waiting to snap a photo as Jerry exited customs. She ran into Jagger’s arms as he cooed, ”Hello babe.” It was all so easy-peasy. I was The Sun’s U.S. correspondent based in Manhattan. After that perfect airport rapprochement, Edwards and I tailed them to Jagger’s chateau near Amboise in the Loire Valley. I had a travel bag with a change of clothes but it was freezing. I swiftly purchased a double-breasted wool and camel hair Burberry overcoat (on expenses — thank you, Rupert Murdoch) which, amazingly, I still have. It’s not in bad nick and it’s perfect for walking the dogs on winter weekends. The aforementioned tale and other crazy memories came flooding back as I watched Danny Boyle ’s scorching new movie Ink , which opens the Venice Film Festival on the Lido on Wednesday. Jack O’Connell as Larry Lamb in ‘Ink’ Anthony Dickenson The film is a sort of origin story for the tabloid papers as we know them today. Jack O’Connell ( Sinners, 28 Years Later ) stars as Larry Lamb, a then-little-known, Yorkshire-born news executive on the U.K.’s biggest selling daily paper, the Daily Mirror. The business-savvy Murdoch approaches Lamb with a plan to relaunch a rival to the Mirror: The Sun newspaper, a middling broadsheet he’s bought for a pittance from Hugh Cudlipp’s IPC publishing group. And this mission suits Lamb just fine, because IPC also owns the Daily Mirror, and Lamb is out for revenge against his employers for not promoting him. Lamb gamely assembles a team of brilliant misfits and The Sun relaunches as a tabloid in November, 1969. O’Connell is superb as the brilliant newspaper tactician Lamb. It’s a huge performance, even Shakespearean in stature, as glory turns to tragedy. In the stage version of Ink , written by James Graham , which premiered in London in 2017, the role of Murdoch was played by Bertie Carvel ( Dalgiesh , Doctor Foster ) and he was magnificent. But for this film incarnation of Graham’s story, Boyle wanted an Australian to portray the man labelled the ‘Dirty Digger’. And Guy Pearce cracks it as the Aussie who beat the Brits at their own game of publishing. Doyle’s ‘big three’ cast is rounded out by Claire Foy ( The Crown, Women Talking ), who is ferociously good as Jules, an amalgam of the group of women Lamb gathered for plumb posts on the Sun. Claire Foy as Jules Davies in ‘Ink’ Anthony Dickenson Boyle introduced Foy to former newspaper editor and columnist Eve Pollard (who happens to be the mother of The Traitors host Claudia Winkleman). “Claire loved her biting wit and modeled herself primarily on Eve and other pioneering Sun women, such as Joyce Hopkirk, who went from being the paper’s first women’s editor to editor of the U.K. Cosmopolitan,” Boyle tells me when we get on the phone to discuss the film. He took Graham’s award-winning play of the same name and spun it into cinema art. “It’s cracking the Magnificent Seven of it. Assembling a bunch of people. They were the underdogs, and Larry and Rupert turned them into all-stars,” Boyle says. The Sun soared. Within months, it was outselling the Mirror and in its heyday, the paper sold four million copies a day. The runaway hit paper was laced with stories about the shenanigans of stars, politicians, footballers, Page 3 girls (back then, topless female models were on every issue’s opening spread), horoscopes, sport, female-aimed features and serializations of books about matters of sex — all with pithy, attention-grabbing headlines, saucy graphics and photos. The paper absolutely revolutionized daily newspaper habits. “It’s taken us to where we are now with the internet,” Boyle says, adding, “we can’t complain about it because we bought it. No one forced us to.” Brian Gleeson, Patrick Kennedy, Claire Foy, Christopher Fulford and Blake Harrison in ‘Ink’ Anthony Dickenson In Darkest Hour , for which Gary Oldman won a Best Actor Oscar for his portrayal of wartime leader Winston Churchill, the great statesman is seen riding on the London Underground — a bit of poetic license. But Murdoch actually did ride around on the tube, checking out which newspapers were being read. “It’s true,” Boyle says. “Back then, he wasn’t the household name he is now. He blended in.” And it was such scenes as this that allowed Boyle and Graham to turn a stage-bound story into a big-screen tale. Boyle studied film adaptations of Peter Shaffer’s Amadeus , which was turned into an Oscar-winning Best Picture by Miloš Forman, and Christopher Hampton’s Les liaisons dangereuses , from which filmmaker Stephen Frears created Dangerous Liaisons , which won three Oscar trophies and was nominated for Best Film. “I looked at them because these two films were based on stage plays but in the hands of Forman and Frears they became pure cinema,” Boyle says. Boyle says he’s in such awe of Frears ( The Queen, The Grifters, Philomena ) that he and others are encouraging the British Film Institute to honor Frears with a “big BFI season” of his movies. Guy Pearce as Murdoch and Jack O’Connell as Lamb in ‘Ink’ Anthony Dickenson When Kelvin MacKenzie took over as The Sun’s editor in 1981, he hired me away from the Evening Standard to become The Sun’s show business and general reporter in London. I covered riots in Brixton, South London, and when there was unrest in Liverpool, MacKenzie ordered teams of reporters to cover the mayhem. But covering movie and rock stars was my main beat. One time, I showed up at Elizabeth Taylor’s pad in Chelsea and handed her a bouquet of flowers. She was huge news in those days. By then, Richard Burton was divorced from Taylor and married to Sally Burton, but still, he turned up for Taylor’s 50th birthday celebrations. So, of course, I followed him. It turned out he was staying at the Dorchester Hotel, where I somehow managed to persuade him to let me inside his suite. As he poured out his heart about “darling Elizabeth” (and poured booze down his throat), I would excuse myself to the bathroom every fifteen minutes to write up notes on the crinkly, hard loo paper. Not to boast (OK, I will), but the resulting spread brought me job offers from rival papers. So, Murdoch and MacKenzie dispatched me to New York to keep the poachers at bay. Talk about fun on the Sun! I had the time of my life! “Joan Collins has a cold. She’s in Los Angeles. Take her flowers and get an interview.” Director Danny Boyle and Jack O’Connell as Lamb on the set of ‘Ink’ Nick Wall “Rod Stewart’s living it up in Hollywood. Go see him.” One day, the instruction came: “Randy Andy (the former Prince Andrew) is on a plane with model Koo Stark bound for Barbados. They’re headed for Mustique, and the Daily Express is with them. Go and join them.” “The local authorities won’t let me stay on the island,” I wailed. “Charter a yacht!” came the reply. But I was also told to share said yacht with rival journalists to cover the costs, mind you. Every morning, we’d row or swim to Basil’s Bar, where we were allowed to avail ourselves of his food and drink, for a price. Island security would corral us at Basil’s. However, a few of us would slope off to try and interact with the prince and his starlet. My photographer Matthew Ford and the Daily Mail’s snapper Peter Carrette were arrested. When we tried to bail them out of jail, Carrette managed to covertly pass me his roll of film. By rights it belonged to the Mail. But I had it, so they had to share. The resulting photo that ran in The Sun of a bare-chested Andrew was headlined Me Tarzan, You Koo. The escapade cost thousands of dollars. The Sun’s managing editor was livid. He still approved my expenses. There were many other such jolly outings in the Caribbean, South America and across the U.S., all with the aim of filling column inches with showbiz and a few actual hard news stories. The thing about The Sun was, they had a crack team of reporters and editing staff who would turn your turn your copy into gold. People used to ask if I was ever embarrassed about working on The Sun. I wasn’t. When I accompanied Andrew from Barbados back to London, a TV newsman interviewed me after I landed at Heathrow and asked me to justify the time and money spent chasing the prince and the showgirl. I simply replied that “I was enjoying myself.” A year or so later, the Daily Mail’s editor David English was in Manhattan. He came a-courting and I switched papers. My days in The Sun were over. Guy Pearce as Murdoch in ‘Ink’ Anthony Dickenson The best movies set in the newspaper world are mostly American ones. Boyle cites Billy Wilder’s Ace in the Hole . And, of course, there’s Alexander Mackendrick’s Sweet Smell of Success , Howard Hawks’ His Girl Friday , Alan J. Pakula’s All the President’s Men and Tom McCarthy’s Spotlight . The only British movie that springs to mind is Val Guest’s The Day the Earth Caught Fire — and now there’s Boyle’s Ink . It joins that list because it’s a portrait of Britain that also reflects aspects of our society now, for good and bad. In Graham’s play Ink , it was Carvel’s larger than life portrayal of Murdoch that seemed to dominate the piece. Graham tells me that Boyle “wanted to slightly tilt the balance” towards what “I think was the surprise in the play — that everyone assumed they were coming to watch a biography of Murdoch, and that Murdoch is the agent of all this change. I think what delighted Danny was the idea that actually no, it’s Larry Lamb, this guy you’ve never heard of, who who drove a lot of those most radical changes and built a lot of what would become the template for modern day populist sensational news. Danny really delights in that.” Boyle says that he was initially apprehensive about seeking out Carvel to play the Mirror’s owner Hugh Cudlipp. “I loved the play and I remembered when I saw Bertie do it, that theater is a celebration of live performance. But for the film, I wanted Bertie to flex different muscles as Cudlipp. I thought he’d kill me when I approached him about Cudlipp. And he did go, ‘Oh, f–k, really?’ But when I explained that I wanted an Australian for Murdoch he understood what I was saying and took Cudlipp and captures him.” But it’s O’Connell’s Lamb that’s at the heart of the film. Boyle thought of Al Pacino in The Godfather Part II when he was working on the script with Graham. “You see Pacino’s Michael Corleone shut out the people closest to him and Lamb does that in Ink . Jack does that. His desire to create this newspaper makes him lose his soul,” Boyle says. Graham notes that what’s liberating for him is “you know everybody has strong feelings about The Sun in particular, and Murdoch’s empire more generally. What’s liberating for us, I guess, is by going back to the beginning, you don’t have to worry about the politics of the now in painting too much on that. You’re basically going, this is how the newspaper was built. This is how it started. Isn’t it quite surprising, actually, that a lot of the people who built it were working class outsiders, often from the north and around the country — a group of people trying to make the news less pompous and less earnest, and make it fun.” But of course, now we’re in an era where everything has changed. 24 hour news and commentary taking over from the facts has only escalated, but also, social media and AI and the platforms in which we share information now are all about engagement. It’s all about distraction and engagement and activation rather than what people might need to hear, or what the boring truth is. And that is worrying. “I think I’m terrified and worried about all those things,” Graham says. And going back to the surprising origins of in The Sun in the 1960s has made him see that the state of how we get our news now is “more urgent than ever.” Ink has its U.S. theatrical release on December 11, U.K. theatrical through StudioCanal is January 8 and it’s on Netflix in the U.S. from January 8. title: Maureen Lipman Tells “Cowardly” Co-Star To “Grow Up” After He Quit Play Over Her Pro-Israel Views
full_text: Skip to main content By Jake Kanter Jake Kanter International Investigations Editor @Jake_Kanter More Stories By Jake Jasmine Jobson Teases Details About Netflix’s ‘Top Boy’ Spin-Off Series ‘Jaq’: “She’s Going Down A Crazy Rabbit Hole” Maureen Lipman Tells “Cowardly” Co-Star To “Grow Up” After He Quit Play Over Her Pro-Israel Views ‘Entourage’ Creator Doug Ellin Denies Debi Mazar’s “Disgusting” Claim About Being Fat-Shamed On HBO Series After Giving Birth View All September 2, 2026 2:00am Maureen Lipman Getty Maureen Lipman , the BAFTA-nominated actress known for her work in The Pianist , has hit out at co-star Gerard McCarthy after he quit their Soho Theatre play over her pro-Israel stance. Lipman and McCarthy were due to share a stage in Stan Zimmerman’s Right Before I Go on September 5, but McCarthy walked away from the project citing Lipman’s political views. In an Instagram post, McCarthy said: “Because of views she has publicly and repeatedly expressed regarding Israel and Palestine, I did not feel comfortable personally promoting her involvement. Related Stories News Maureen Lipman Attacks BAFTA "Numbskulls" Over Gender-Neutral Award Engravings News UK March Against Antisemitism Attended By Maureen Lipman, Eddie Marsan, Boris Johnson “I did not ask for her casting to be reconsidered or expect anyone else to share my position. I simply chose not to use my own platform to promote someone whose political views are at odds with my own.” Watch on Deadline View this post on Instagram Responding in The Times of London , Lipman described McCarthy as “cowardly” for quitting the play without speaking to her directly. She said his Instagram post was “virtue-signalling” and called on the actor, who has appeared in The Fall , to “grow up.” “I am asking for him to have the courage to face me and tell me what he thinks it is I should do, or think, or say,” she said. “I would like to reassure him that I will not be arriving with a star of David on my forehead, nor am I trying to argue him out of his point of view. “He has to wake up and smell the grass. I have worked with actors for 60 years who often don’t share my politics. I don’t ask them, and they don’t ask me.” Lipman added that McCarthy’s position was curious given it came just weeks after he attended the opening night of Richmond Theatre’s production of Allegra , in which the Olivier Award-winning actress was the lead. McCarthy posed for a photo in front of a poster featuring Lipman’s name in large print. Gerard McCarthy “I would love to know what has changed in the last six weeks. Has he become radicalised, and by whom?” Lipman said. “I am at a loss, but I would like to extend the olive branch and get a proper understanding of his problem with me. “I am simply a working woman of a certain age who believes that the state of Israel should be allowed to exist. I am an actor, not a politician. There is very little I can do to influence (Israeli prime minister) Bibi Netanyahu, nor would I want to.” McCarthy has been approached for comment. Lipman, 80, supports Israel’s right to exist and defend itself, and has previously been critical of artists who publicly back Palestine without mentioning Hamas. title: ‘Bunker’: Watch Javier Bardem & Penélope Cruz In Florian Zeller’s Venice-Bound Psychological Thriller
full_text: Skip to main content By Diana Lodderhose Diana Lodderhose International Features Editor @dianalodderhose More Stories By Diana Cynthia Erivo, Andrew Scott, Ava DuVernay, Jesse Eisenberg & More Set For London Film Festival Screen Talks Program Tom Hiddleston Thriller ‘Tenzing’ To Open Zurich Film Festival Marketing Executive Kevin Harrington Launches New Entertainment Agency Patrick Patrick View All September 2, 2026 2:17am EXCLUSIVE : Here’s an exclusive clip from Florian Zeller’s upcoming Venice competition title Bunker starring Penélope Cruz and Javier Bardem . The psychological thriller, which Zeller wrote, produced and directed, follows the emotional and moral challenges faced by a couple in an increasingly uncertain world. Bardem plays Miguel, a successful London architect, who considers a prestigious offer to build a survivalist bunker for a tech billionaire. The project causes his wife Sofia (Cruz) to question their relationship of 17 years as they are drawn deeper into a life of extreme wealth, paranoia and fear. The intrusion of an unsettling neighbor becomes another source of anxiety. The French-Spanish co-production is produced by Federica Sainte-Rose, Zeller for Blue Morning Pictures, Fernando Bovaira and Simon de Santiago of MOD Producciones and Alice Dawson. Pathé’s Ardavan Safaee and Mediawan’s Pierre-Antoine Capton serve as co-producers. Earlier this year, Sony Pictures Classics acquired North American, Southeast Asian and worldwide airline rights (excluding France) for the title. The film continues SPC’s relationship with Zeller that dates back to the release of his first film, Oscar winner The Father , and his second film The Son . FilmNation Entertainment is handling international sales on the film while CAA Media Finance and WME repped domestic rights. Pathé is set to distribute the film in France, Switzerland and West Africa. Bunker is set to world premiere In Competition at the Venice International Film Festival on September 8. title: Jean-Paul Rappeneau Dies: ‘Cyrano de Bergerac’ Director Was 94
full_text: Skip to main content By Melanie Goodfellow Melanie Goodfellow Senior International Film Correspondent @mel_goodfellow More Stories By Melanie Venice Jury Head Maggie Gyllenhaal Calls For Empathy In Politically Charged Times; Addresses Dearth Of Women In Competition: “It’s A Systemic Problem” Jean-Paul Rappeneau Dies: ‘Cyrano de Bergerac’ Director Was 94 Ukrainian Drama ‘Camouflage’ Set Sales With MMM Films – Venice View All September 2, 2026 2:22am Jean-Paul Rappeneau at Romy Schneider Exhibition At La Cinematheque In Paris in 2023 Getty Images French director and screenwriter Jean-Paul Rappeneau , who was best known internationally for the 1990 Oscar-nominated drama Cyrano de Bergerac , died on September 2 his family has announced. He was 94. Born on April 8, 1932 in the town of Auxerre in central France , Rappeneau’s career spanned more than 50 years of French cinema history. His early screenwriting credits include Louis Malle’s Zazie in the Metro ((1960)and A Very Private Affair (1962) as well as Philippe de Broca’s classic thriller That Man From Rio starring Jean-Paul Belmondo. Related Stories News Donald Trump Pays Tribute To Dolly Parton, Says He's Lowering U.S. Flags To Honor Entertainer News Saudi Arabia To Invest $7 Billion In Three Theme Parks Near Paris He broke into feature film directing in 1966 with A Matter of Resistance , a romantic comedy set on the eve of France’s World War Two liberation starring Catherine Deneuve. Watch on Deadline The pair would work together again on his 1975 film Le Sauvage , co-starring Yves Montand as a man living a solitary on a Caribbean island who becomes entangled with a runaway bride. Other directorial credits include All Fired Up (1982) and Horseman on the Roof (1995). He is best known internationally, however, for his big screen adaptation of Edmond Rostand’s 1897 stage play Cyrano de Bergerac starring Gerard Depardieu in the titular role. After world premiering in 1990 in Cannes, where Depardieu won Best Actor, the film enjoyed a buzzy awards season garnering five nominations in the lead up to the 63rd Academy Awards, including for Best Actor and Best Foreign Language Film. It missed out on both prizes, but won Best Costume Design for Franca Squarciapino. Rappeneau’s last feature-length directorial credit was the comedy drama Families starring Mathieu Amalric as a Shanghai-based French financier who returns home to find the family mansion is being sold off.
